title: Angular Native Federation Fundamentals
text: Day 272 — Angular Native Federation Fundamentals Goal Learn host, remote, exposed capability, remote entry, shared dependency, and federation configuration concepts. Build a small host plus Candidate remote proof of concept. Concepts Identify the architectural boundary before selecting federation tooling. Keep contracts small, typed, and intentionally versioned. Keep business ownership inside the remote that owns the capability. Share platform capabilities deliberately rather than sharing all implementation details. Treat runtime configuration, deployment, observability, rollback, security, and performance as part of the architecture. JobHub Exercise Apply today's concept to JobHub. Document the host/remote boundary, dependency direction, communication contract, failure behavior, and major trade offs. Common Mistakes Introducing MFE only because an application is large. Sharing every dependency or service. Letting remotes import each other's internals. Treating the remote boundary as a security boundary. Ignoring deployment, caching, rollback, or performance. Angular 21 + Native Federation Version Note Native Federation is provided by the third party package; it is not an Angular framework API. Pin and test a package version compatible with the Angular version used by the workspace rather than copying an unpinned command from an old tutorial. For this curriculum, Angular 21 is the baseline. Verify the package's current compatibility matrix/release notes before installing. A typical Angular setup uses the package's schematic, for example: bash ng add @angular architects/native federation project shell type dynamic host and a remote: bash ng add @angular architects/native federation project candidate type remote The exact generated configuration belongs to the installed package version. Teach the architecture first; do not assume every generated filename or option is permanent. Native Federation uses browser native ES modules/import maps and integrates with Angular's CLI/build tooling. It is distinct from webpack Module Federation, although the architectural mental model is similar. Version Safe Rule Always verify: Angular version; Native Federation package version; Node version; generated CLI/build configuration; shared dependency compatibility. Do not copy configuration from a Native Federation article written for another major version without checking its release documentation.

title: Remote Routes, Components and Contracts
text: Day 273 — Remote Routes, Components and Contracts Goal Design small stable contracts using routes, exposed components, typed inputs and outputs, URL state, and explicit interfaces. Avoid exposing remote internals. Concepts Identify the architectural boundary before selecting federation tooling. Keep contracts small, typed, and intentionally versioned. Keep business ownership inside the remote that owns the capability. Share platform capabilities deliberately rather than sharing all implementation details. Treat runtime configuration, deployment, observability, rollback, security, and performance as part of the architecture. JobHub Exercise Apply today's concept to JobHub. Document the host/remote boundary, dependency direction, communication contract, failure behavior, and major trade offs. Common Mistakes Introducing MFE only because an application is large. Sharing every dependency or service. Letting remotes import each other's internals. Treating the remote boundary as a security boundary. Ignoring deployment, caching, rollback, or performance. Version Safe Remote Loading The exact overloads and generated configuration can vary by Native Federation release. Treat the installed package's TypeScript types and current documentation as the source of truth. The architectural pattern remains stable: ts { path: 'candidate', loadComponent: () = loadRemoteModule('candidate', './Component') .then(m = m.AppComponent), } For a remote owned route tree, expose a routing contract and lazy load it from the host. Keep the exposed name stable even if the remote's internal file structure changes. Do not expose arbitrary internal services, stores, or implementation files merely because federation makes them technically loadable.

title: Shared Dependencies and Version Strategy
text: Day 274 — Shared Dependencies and Version Strategy Goal Understand dependency sharing trade offs, singleton behavior, version compatibility, upgrade frequency, and public platform contracts. Create a JobHub dependency sharing matrix. Concepts Identify the architectural boundary before selecting federation tooling. Keep contracts small, typed, and intentionally versioned. Keep business ownership inside the remote that owns the capability. Share platform capabilities deliberately rather than sharing all implementation details. Treat runtime configuration, deployment, observability, rollback, security, and performance as part of the architecture. JobHub Exercise Apply today's concept to JobHub. Document the host/remote boundary, dependency direction, communication contract, failure behavior, and major trade offs. Common Mistakes Introducing MFE only because an application is large. Sharing every dependency or service. Letting remotes import each other's internals. Treating the remote boundary as a security boundary. Ignoring deployment, caching, rollback, or performance. Native Federation Dependency Sharing Shared dependencies are a runtime compatibility decision, not simply a bundle size optimization. For Angular applications, commonly shared platform dependencies may include Angular packages and other libraries that must behave as singletons. The exact configuration syntax is package version specific. A useful policy is: 1. share only dependencies that benefit from sharing; 2. keep Angular package versions compatible across host/remotes; 3. test singleton behavior for libraries that maintain registries or global state; 4. avoid sharing feature specific business libraries unless there is a deliberate contract; 5. review dependency upgrades as a platform change. Do not blindly use forever. It can be convenient for learning, but production architectures should understand what is actually being shared. Angular 21 Rule Do not assume an older , , or sharing option has identical behavior in every Native Federation release. Verify the generated configuration and package documentation for the installed version.

title: Shared UI, Services and Authentication
text: Day 275 — Shared UI, Services and Authentication Goal Design shared platform capabilities such as design system UI, authentication contracts, permission contracts, telemetry, notifications, and configuration while avoiding shared business state coupling. Concepts Identify the architectural boundary before selecting federation tooling. Keep contracts small, typed, and intentionally versioned. Keep business ownership inside the remote that owns the capability. Share platform capabilities deliberately rather than sharing all implementation details. Treat runtime configuration, deployment, observability, rollback, security, and performance as part of the architecture. JobHub Exercise Apply today's concept to JobHub. Document the host/remote boundary, dependency direction, communication contract, failure behavior, and major trade offs. Common Mistakes Introducing MFE only because an application is large. Sharing every dependency or service. Letting remotes import each other's internals. Treating the remote boundary as a security boundary. Ignoring deployment, caching, rollback, or performance. Shared Platform Boundary Prefer sharing contracts and platform capabilities over sharing mutable business state. Good candidates: design system components; authentication/session contract; permission contract; telemetry; notifications; runtime configuration. Avoid creating a global "everything service" consumed by every remote. Authentication is also not a security boundary. A remote must not rely only on host provided UI state for authorization. Backend authorization remains authoritative. Version Note If the host and remote share Angular services or libraries, verify that the installed Native Federation version supports the intended sharing model and that the shared packages are compatible. Do not assume an example from an older major release remains configuration compatible.

title: Runtime Configuration and Environment-Aware Remote Loading
text: Day 276 — Runtime Configuration and Environment Aware Remote Loading Goal Separate build time and runtime deployment configuration. Design environment aware remote URLs and remote unavailable fallback behavior. Browser configuration is not a secret store. Concepts Identify the architectural boundary before selecting federation tooling. Keep contracts small, typed, and intentionally versioned. Keep business ownership inside the remote that owns the capability. Share platform capabilities deliberately rather than sharing all implementation details. Treat runtime configuration, deployment, observability, rollback, security, and performance as part of the architecture. JobHub Exercise Apply today's concept to JobHub. Document the host/remote boundary, dependency direction, communication contract, failure behavior, and major trade offs. Common Mistakes Introducing MFE only because an application is large. Sharing every dependency or service. Letting remotes import each other's internals. Treating the remote boundary as a security boundary. Ignoring deployment, caching, rollback, or performance. Runtime Manifest Pattern A dynamic host can keep remote locations in runtime configuration so the same build can be promoted across environments. Conceptually: json { "candidate": "https://example.com/candidate/remoteEntry.json", "recruiter": "https://example.com/recruiter/remoteEntry.json" } The exact manifest filename and loading API depend on the installed Native Federation release. Treat this configuration as public browser configuration. Remote URLs are not secrets . Validate remote configuration before loading it and define a user visible fallback when a remote is unavailable. Angular 21 / Package Version Rule Do not hard code a Native Federation configuration format from a different major version. Generate or inspect the configuration for the installed package, then adapt the runtime configuration to that generated contract.

title: Navigation, Communication and Cross-MFE Events
text: Day 277 — Navigation, Communication and Cross MFE Events Goal Use the smallest communication mechanism that works: URL state, direct inputs and outputs, typed contracts, explicit events, and shared state only when ownership is truly cross application. Concepts Identify the architectural boundary before selecting federation tooling. Keep contracts small, typed, and intentionally versioned. Keep business ownership inside the remote that owns the capability. Share platform capabilities deliberately rather than sharing all implementation details. Treat runtime configuration, deployment, observability, rollback, security, and performance as part of the architecture. JobHub Exercise Apply today's concept to JobHub. Document the host/remote boundary, dependency direction, communication contract, failure behavior, and major trade offs. Common Mistakes Introducing MFE only because an application is large. Sharing every dependency or service. Letting remotes import each other's internals. Treating the remote boundary as a security boundary. Ignoring deployment, caching, rollback, or performance. Communication Hierarchy Use the smallest contract that solves the problem: 1. URL/path/query parameters for navigable state; 2. component inputs/outputs when the relationship is direct; 3. typed custom events for explicit cross MFE notifications; 4. shared platform services for truly cross application concerns; 5. shared state only when ownership is genuinely application wide. Avoid making every remote subscribe to every other remote. Version Note Native Federation does not remove Angular routing or browser communication rules. The exact helper APIs for loading a remote can change between package releases; keep communication contracts independent from those implementation details.

title: Deployment, Caching and Failure Isolation
text: Day 278 — Deployment, Caching and Failure Isolation Goal Plan independent remote deployment, asset caching, compatibility, rollback, and failure isolation. Test unavailable remotes, network failures, invalid configuration, and incompatible contracts. Concepts Identify the architectural boundary before selecting federation tooling. Keep contracts small, typed, and intentionally versioned. Keep business ownership inside the remote that owns the capability. Share platform capabilities deliberately rather than sharing all implementation details. Treat runtime configuration, deployment, observability, rollback, security, and performance as part of the architecture. JobHub Exercise Apply today's concept to JobHub. Document the host/remote boundary, dependency direction, communication contract, failure behavior, and major trade offs. Common Mistakes Introducing MFE only because an application is large. Sharing every dependency or service. Letting remotes import each other's internals. Treating the remote boundary as a security boundary. Ignoring deployment, caching, rollback, or performance. Deployment Contract Treat each remote as an independently deployable artifact with: immutable/versioned assets where practical; a compatible remote manifest; cache control appropriate for the asset type; rollback to a known compatible version; health/error telemetry; a host fallback. Do not deploy a host that requires a remote version that has already been deleted. Failure Scenarios Test: remote URL unavailable; remote manifest invalid; network timeout; remote JavaScript failure; incompatible shared dependency; incompatible exposed contract. A micro frontend improves deployment independence only when the contracts and release process support that independence. Native Federation Version Note The generated build/start/deployment artifacts are package version specific. Verify the installed Native Federation release's production startup instructions instead of copying an old , , or manifest workflow blindly.

title: Micro Frontend Performance, Security and Governance
text: Day 279 — Micro Frontend Performance, Security and Governance Goal Measure startup, remote loading, duplicated dependencies, navigation latency, network requests, and caching. Review CSP, authentication, authorization, supply chain, observability, ownership, and release governance. Concepts Identify the architectural boundary before selecting federation tooling. Keep contracts small, typed, and intentionally versioned. Keep business ownership inside the remote that owns the capability. Share platform capabilities deliberately rather than sharing all implementation details. Treat runtime configuration, deployment, observability, rollback, security, and performance as part of the architecture. JobHub Exercise Apply today's concept to JobHub. Document the host/remote boundary, dependency direction, communication contract, failure behavior, and major trade offs. Common Mistakes Introducing MFE only because an application is large. Sharing every dependency or service. Letting remotes import each other's internals. Treating the remote boundary as a security boundary. Ignoring deployment, caching, rollback, or performance. Performance Measurement Measure: initial host JavaScript; manifest/import map work; remote network requests; remote execution time; duplicated dependencies; route transition latency; cache hit/miss behavior. Do not assume federation automatically improves performance. Runtime composition can add network and startup overhead. Security A remote is not a trust boundary. Treat remote code as application code with the same security consequences as host code. Review: CSP; authentication and authorization; dependency/supply chain risk; remote integrity and deployment controls; sensitive runtime configuration; observability and incident response. Governance Define: ownership per remote; supported Angular/package versions; contract compatibility policy; release/rollback policy; deprecation policy; performance budgets. Native Federation version changes should be treated as platform changes and validated across all host/remotes.

title: Mini Project — Enterprise JobHub Micro Frontends
text: Day 280 — Mini Project — Enterprise JobHub Micro Frontends Goal Build a JobHub host with Candidate, Recruiter, and Admin remotes. Implement route based loading, explicit contracts, runtime remote configuration, shared platform capabilities, fallback states, deployment ownership, rollback planning, and performance measurement. Concepts Identify the architectural boundary before selecting federation tooling. Keep contracts small, typed, and intentionally versioned. Keep business ownership inside the remote that owns the capability. Share platform capabilities deliberately rather than sharing all implementation details. Treat runtime configuration, deployment, observability, rollback, security, and performance as part of the architecture. JobHub Exercise Apply today's concept to JobHub. Document the host/remote boundary, dependency direction, communication contract, failure behavior, and major trade offs. Common Mistakes Introducing MFE only because an application is large. Sharing every dependency or service. Letting remotes import each other's internals. Treating the remote boundary as a security boundary. Ignoring deployment, caching, rollback, or performance. Version Safe Implementation Rule Use Angular 21 as the curriculum baseline and select a currently compatible release before implementation. Record the exact versions in the project README/package manifest. Do not mix configuration copied from multiple Native Federation major versions. Implementation Create: Host Candidate remote Recruiter remote Admin remote The host owns: application shell; authentication bootstrap; global navigation; runtime remote configuration; shared platform contracts; remote failure UX. Each remote owns its domain UI and business behavior. Acceptance Tests Verify: each remote loads independently; a remote can fail without blanking the entire host; route contracts remain stable; shared Angular dependencies are compatible; runtime URLs can change without rebuilding the host; authenticated authorization remains backend controlled; remote loading and navigation performance are measured. Architecture Review Document the exact Native Federation package version, Angular version, shared dependencies, exposed contracts, runtime manifest format, deployment strategy, rollback strategy, and known limitations. The purpose is not merely to make three remotes load. The learner must be able to explain why the boundaries exist and how version changes are managed.

title: day-281-final-project-vision-requirements-and-architecture
text: Day 281 — Final Project Vision, Requirements and Architecture Define the enterprise JobHub capstone, personas, scope, success criteria and architecture. Map the project to the Angular skills learned so far. Goal Turn the earlier JobHub work into one production style application that integrates Angular fundamentals, modern reactivity, forms, HTTP, state management, testing, performance, security, SSR and micro frontends. Project Scope JobHub has Candidate, Recruiter and Admin experiences. A lightweight host composes independently deployable feature frontends. Backend APIs may be real or contract driven/mock during development. Architecture Angular standalone application model Feature/domain boundaries Signals and SignalStore where shared complexity requires it HttpClient/httpResource for data access where appropriate RxJS only for genuinely stream oriented workflows Native Federation for remote feature applications Vitest for automated tests Responsive, accessible and secure UI Exercise Create a requirements checklist and draw the runtime architecture before writing feature code. Common Mistakes Starting with components before defining boundaries; putting all state in a global store; coupling remotes through internal implementation details; treating browser configuration as a secret store. Interview Questions 1. What makes this an enterprise application rather than a large component demo? 2. How would you decide whether a capability belongs in the host or a remote? 3. Which boundaries should remain stable as the project grows? Outcome You have a written architecture and implementation backlog for the final JobHub project. Prerequisites Complete Days 1–280. This capstone assumes the learner already knows Angular fundamentals, Signals, forms, HTTP, RxJS, state management, testing, performance, SSR/hydration, security, enterprise architecture, and Micro Frontends. Acceptance Criteria Before implementation begins, the team can explain each major technology choice in terms of a concrete requirement, identify ownership boundaries, and describe how Candidate, Recruiter, and Admin workflows are separated. Challenge For every major technology in the architecture, answer: What concrete requirement makes this technology necessary? If there is no clear answer, do not add the technology merely for demonstration.

title: day-282-repository-and-application-setup
text: Day 282 — Repository and Application Setup Set up the repositories, Angular applications, environments, package conventions and development workflow for the capstone. Goal Create a repeatable foundation for the host and Candidate, Recruiter and Admin applications. Setup Areas Angular standalone projects TypeScript strictness routing and application configuration lint/format conventions environment and runtime configuration boundaries local development commands test setup with Vitest source control and commit conventions Exercise Create a minimal host and one feature application. Verify local builds, tests and navigation before adding business functionality. Common Mistakes Copying production configuration into source control; adding dependencies before defining ownership; skipping a clean baseline build and test run. Interview Questions 1. What should be established before feature development begins? 2. Which configuration belongs at build time versus runtime? 3. Why is a reproducible development setup important? Outcome The capstone has a clean, repeatable application foundation.

title: day-283-enterprise-design-system-and-application-shell
text: Day 283 — Enterprise Design System and Application Shell Build the shared visual language and lightweight application shell used by the enterprise JobHub experience. Goal Create stable shared UI contracts without turning shared UI into a business logic dumping ground. Design System typography and spacing tokens buttons, inputs, cards and feedback states navigation shell responsive layout loading, empty and error primitives accessible interaction patterns theme/configuration boundaries Exercise Implement the shell and a small reusable UI kit. Document which components are platform level and which remain feature owned. Common Mistakes Putting feature specific workflows in shared components; excessive component abstraction; styling that depends on remote internals. Interview Questions 1. What makes a shared component a good platform contract? 2. How do you prevent a shared UI library from becoming a bottleneck? 3. What belongs in an application shell? Outcome The project has a consistent, accessible shell with explicit shared UI boundaries.

title: day-284-authentication-session-bootstrap-and-authorization
text: Day 284 — Authentication, Session Bootstrap and Authorization Integrate authentication bootstrap, session state and permission aware application behavior. Goal Make protected application experiences work consistently across the host and feature applications. Architecture session bootstrap authentication state route protection role and permission checks authenticated API requests session expiry handling backend authorization as the final authority Exercise Implement a login/session flow using a contract or mock API, then protect Candidate, Recruiter and Admin capabilities with explicit permissions. Common Mistakes Relying only on frontend authorization; storing secrets in browser configuration; scattering token logic across components. Interview Questions 1. What is the difference between authentication and authorization? 2. Why can frontend guards never replace backend authorization? 3. Where should authentication behavior be centralized? Outcome The application has a coherent authentication and authorization boundary.

title: day-285-runtime-configuration-and-environment-strategy
text: Day 285 — Runtime Configuration and Environment Strategy Separate application code from environment specific deployment configuration. Goal Make the same build capable of running against different environments where the deployment architecture requires runtime configuration. Configuration Areas API base URLs remote application URLs feature flags environment metadata safe public client configuration configuration validation and fallback behavior Exercise Create a typed runtime configuration contract consumed by the host and remote loading layer. Test missing and invalid configuration paths. Common Mistakes Hardcoding production URLs; treating public browser configuration as secret; duplicating configuration parsing in multiple features. Interview Questions 1. What is the difference between build time and runtime configuration? 2. Why should browser visible configuration never contain secrets? 3. How should invalid configuration fail? Outcome Deployment configuration is explicit, typed and centralized.

title: day-286-candidate-experience-job-search-and-discovery
text: Day 286 — Candidate Experience — Job Search and Discovery Build the Candidate job discovery workflow with filtering, sorting, pagination and responsive UI states. Goal Create a realistic job search experience using the project's data access and state patterns. Features search by keyword/location filters and sorting loading, empty and error states pagination or incremental loading typed API models URL query state where useful Exercise Implement the workflow from route entry to API request to rendered results. Keep server data, UI state and form state clearly separated. Common Mistakes Triggering requests directly from many components; losing filter state during navigation; rendering large lists without tracking strategy. Interview Questions 1. Which state belongs in the URL? 2. When would RxJS be useful in search interactions? 3. How would you prevent unnecessary API requests? Outcome Candidates can efficiently search and discover jobs through a production style workflow.

title: day-287-candidate-experience-job-details-saved-jobs-and-applications
text: Day 287 — Candidate Experience — Job Details, Saved Jobs and Applications Complete the Candidate workflow from job details through saving and applying. Goal Connect detail views, user actions, forms and API state without creating hidden coupling. Features route based job details saved jobs application form validation and submission states success/error feedback navigation after actions Exercise Build the complete application journey and test refresh, back navigation, invalid forms and failed API requests. Common Mistakes Mixing API models directly into every template; losing selected job identity; disabling UX feedback during asynchronous work. Interview Questions 1. Where should application state live? 2. How should a failed submission affect form state? 3. How do route parameters and API data work together? Outcome The Candidate experience supports a complete job application journey.

title: day-288-recruiter-experience-job-management
text: Day 288 — Recruiter Experience — Job Management Build Recruiter job creation, editing, publishing and management workflows. Goal Use Angular forms, validation, HTTP, permissions and feature state in a realistic business workflow. Features recruiter job list create/edit forms validation draft/published status optimistic or confirmed UI updates where justified permission aware actions Exercise Implement the Recruiter workflow using focused feature components and a dedicated data access boundary. Common Mistakes One giant form component; duplicating validation rules; updating UI before understanding API failure semantics. Interview Questions 1. How would you structure a complex feature form? 2. When is optimistic UI appropriate? 3. Where should business rules be enforced? Outcome Recruiters can manage job postings through a structured feature boundary.

title: day-289-recruiter-experience-candidate-and-application-management
text: Day 289 — Recruiter Experience — Candidate and Application Management Build recruiter workflows for reviewing applications and candidate progress. Goal Handle richer collections, filters, details and state transitions without creating feature wide global state unnecessarily. Features application list candidate details status transitions filtering and sorting notes or review metadata permission aware actions Exercise Implement a recruiter application workspace and model its state ownership explicitly before choosing SignalStore state. Common Mistakes Putting every table interaction into global state; coupling candidate screens to recruiter list internals; missing failure recovery. Interview Questions 1. Which state is transient and which is shared? 2. How would you model status transitions safely? 3. How do you keep a feature testable? Outcome Recruiters can review and manage candidate applications with clear state boundaries.

title: day-290-admin-experience-users-roles-and-permissions
text: Day 290 — Admin Experience — Users, Roles and Permissions Build the Admin workspace for users, roles and permission management. Goal Demonstrate enterprise authorization concepts through a realistic administration feature. Features user list and search role assignment permission display guarded administrative actions confirmation and error states audit oriented UI boundaries Exercise Create an Admin feature with explicit permission checks and API contracts. Treat the server as authoritative for every protected mutation. Common Mistakes Hiding a button and assuming that is security; allowing arbitrary role values; sharing admin business logic with unrelated features. Interview Questions 1. What is RBAC? 2. Why are permissions more granular than roles? 3. How should unauthorized API responses be handled? Outcome The project contains a realistic permission aware Admin workspace.

title: day-291-enterprise-state-architecture-and-data-flow
text: Day 291 — Enterprise State Architecture and Data Flow Unify local state, feature state, server data, form state and cross application state using explicit ownership rules. Goal Prevent the capstone from becoming a single global state application. State Rules component state for local UI feature state for coordinated feature workflows SignalStore for meaningful feature complexity server state owned by data access/cache patterns forms own editable form state URL owns navigational state cross MFE state kept minimal and contractual Exercise Create a state map for Candidate, Recruiter and Admin. For every state item, document owner, source, consumers and update mechanism. Common Mistakes Globalizing everything; duplicating server state; deriving the same state in multiple stores. Interview Questions 1. How do you decide where state belongs? 2. What problem does a facade or feature store solve? 3. Why is cross MFE global state risky? Outcome The capstone has predictable state ownership and data flow.

title: day-292-api-data-access-and-error-boundaries
text: Day 292 — API, Data Access and Error Boundaries Harden the API layer with typed contracts, request handling, error mapping and feature level recovery. Goal Keep HTTP concerns out of presentation components and make failures understandable to users and developers. Architecture typed request/response contracts data access services interceptors where cross cutting behavior is appropriate domain/UI model mapping normalized error handling loading/empty/error states retry only when safe Exercise Trace one Candidate, Recruiter and Admin request from UI action to API and back. Document every boundary. Common Mistakes Catching every error and hiding it; retrying mutations blindly; exposing backend DTO details everywhere. Interview Questions 1. Where should API to UI mapping happen? 2. Which errors should be retried? 3. What belongs in an HTTP interceptor versus a feature service? Outcome The API architecture is typed, testable and resilient to expected failures.

title: day-293-micro-frontend-integration-and-remote-contracts
text: Day 293 — Micro Frontend Integration and Remote Contracts Compose the Candidate, Recruiter and Admin applications through the host using stable remote contracts. Goal Apply the MFE architecture from Module 24 to the final project. Integration host shell remote route loading stable public entry points route contracts shared dependency strategy remote loading fallback independent application ownership Exercise Integrate the three feature remotes one at a time. Verify that a remote failure does not make unrelated host functionality unusable. Common Mistakes Exposing internal files as public contracts; tightly coupling remotes; loading every remote during initial startup. Interview Questions 1. What is a remote contract? 2. Why should the host remain lightweight? 3. How should a remote loading failure be represented? Outcome JobHub is composed as a resilient multi application system.

title: day-294-shared-ui-auth-and-platform-contracts
text: Day 294 — Shared UI, Auth and Platform Contracts Stabilize the contracts used by the host and remotes for UI, authentication and platform capabilities. Goal Share only capabilities that genuinely need consistency across applications. Shared Capabilities design system components session/auth contract notifications configuration access navigation primitives telemetry hooks Exercise Review every shared dependency and classify it as platform capability, business capability or feature implementation. Move business logic out of shared platform code. Common Mistakes Creating a shared business store; exposing private component APIs; versioning shared packages without a compatibility plan. Interview Questions 1. What should never become a shared MFE dependency? 2. How do shared contracts affect independent deployment? 3. How can shared platform code remain backward compatible? Outcome Host/remotes share a small, intentional platform contract.

title: day-295-performance-optimization-and-observability
text: Day 295 — Performance Optimization and Observability Measure and improve startup, navigation, rendering, remote loading and API behavior. Goal Use evidence rather than assumptions to optimize the enterprise application. Review route lazy loading @defer boundaries @for tracking signal driven rendering zoneless behavior where enabled remote loading cost network waterfalls caching browser performance profiles structured application telemetry Exercise Capture a baseline, identify the highest cost workflow, make targeted changes and record before/after measurements. Common Mistakes Optimizing without measurement; deferring critical UI; logging sensitive data; adding telemetry everywhere without a useful question. Interview Questions 1. How do you find the real performance bottleneck? 2. What should be measured for an MFE application? 3. What information should never be logged? Outcome The project has measured performance improvements and actionable observability.

title: day-296-accessibility-security-and-ux-hardening
text: Day 296 — Accessibility, Security and UX Hardening Perform the final quality pass across accessibility, security and failure oriented user experience. Goal Treat non functional requirements as part of feature completion. Checklist semantic HTML and keyboard navigation focus management accessible names and states responsive layouts XSS safe rendering secure authentication/session behavior CSP/Trusted Types where deployment supports them safe handling of sensitive data unauthorized and expired session UX loading, empty, error and offline aware states where appropriate Exercise Audit one complete workflow with keyboard only navigation and a security review checklist. Fix issues at the architecture level when possible. Common Mistakes Using ARIA to compensate for incorrect HTML; trusting client side authorization; logging tokens or personal data; ignoring error states. Interview Questions 1. What is progressive enhancement for accessibility? 2. Why is security a system concern rather than a component concern? 3. How should sensitive data be treated in frontend logs? Outcome The capstone is more usable, secure and resilient.

title: day-297-testing-strategy-and-automated-test-suite
text: Day 297 — Testing Strategy and Automated Test Suite Create a layered automated test suite for the final JobHub application. Goal Verify business behavior and integration boundaries without making tests brittle. Coverage services and data access components and user interaction forms and validation signals and feature state HTTP requests routing and guards shared UI contracts MFE integration boundaries where practical Exercise Write tests around critical Candidate application, Recruiter publishing and Admin permission workflows. Run the suite in CI mode. Common Mistakes Testing implementation details; snapshot heavy tests with little behavior coverage; mocking everything; ignoring failed requests. Interview Questions 1. What should a frontend test prove? 2. When should you use TestBed? 3. How do you test HttpClient without calling a real backend? Outcome Critical JobHub workflows are protected by a maintainable Vitest suite.

title: day-298-ci-cd-deployment-and-release-strategy
text: Day 298 — CI/CD, Deployment and Release Strategy Prepare the enterprise project for automated validation and independent deployment. Goal Make every application buildable, testable and releasable through a repeatable pipeline. Pipeline dependency installation lint/static checks unit tests production builds artifact creation security/dependency checks environment configuration deployment smoke verification rollback strategy MFE Release Concerns Remotes should be deployable independently, while the host must remain compatible with published remote contracts. Exercise Define a release pipeline for host and each remote and document how a failed remote release is rolled back. Common Mistakes Coupling all deployments into one release; publishing untested remote contracts; storing secrets in repository configuration. Interview Questions 1. What makes an MFE deployment independent? 2. How do you handle incompatible remote contracts? 3. What should happen when production deployment succeeds but a remote is unhealthy? Outcome JobHub has a documented, repeatable CI/CD and release strategy.

title: day-299-production-readiness-review-and-refactoring
text: Day 299 — Production Readiness Review and Refactoring Review the complete application as a production system and refactor where boundaries or behavior are weak. Goal Find architectural debt before the final demo. Review Areas feature boundaries dependency direction state ownership shared contracts error handling accessibility security performance tests configuration deployment documentation Exercise Create a production readiness checklist. Refactor at least three concrete issues and explain why each change improves maintainability or reliability. Common Mistakes Refactoring only for aesthetics; changing architecture without evidence; leaving known test or build failures for the demo. Interview Questions 1. How do you identify architectural debt? 2. When should you refactor versus accept technical debt? 3. What evidence would you require before calling an application production ready? Outcome The final system has undergone an explicit architecture and production readiness review.

title: day-300-final-enterprise-jobhub-demo-and-architecture-walkthrough
text: Day 300 — Final Enterprise JobHub Demo and Architecture Walkthrough Goal Present JobHub as an end to end enterprise Angular project and explain its architecture from browser entry to feature workflow and deployment. Demo Flow 1. Host shell and session bootstrap 2. Candidate job search and application 3. Recruiter job management and candidate review 4. Admin users, roles and permissions 5. Remote loading and failure fallback 6. API/data access flow 7. State ownership and SignalStore usage 8. Accessibility and responsive behavior 9. Tests and CI/CD 10. Performance, security and observability review Architecture Walkthrough Explain boundaries, contracts, state ownership, rendering strategy, configuration, deployment and tradeoffs. Be explicit about what is shared and what is independently owned. Final Exercise Record a short architecture walkthrough and create a final project README containing setup, architecture, local development, testing, deployment and key decisions. Interview Questions 1. Walk through the complete JobHub architecture. 2. Why did you choose each state management boundary? 3. How does the application remain resilient when a remote fails? 4. How would you evolve this architecture as teams and domains grow? Outcome You have a portfolio and interview ready enterprise Angular capstone that connects the major concepts from Days 1–299.

text: Day 1 — Angular Interview Questions Topic What is Angular and Why Angular? Interview Goal By the end of this interview practice, the learner should be able to explain Angular in simple language, describe why a framework is useful, and distinguish Angular from plain JavaScript and other frontend approaches. Level 1 — Basic Questions Q1. What is Angular? Expected Answer: Angular is a TypeScript based web application framework developed by Google for building scalable client side applications. It provides built in solutions for common application needs such as components, templates, routing, forms, dependency injection, HTTP communication, and testing. Q2. Is Angular a library or a framework? Expected Answer: Angular is a framework. It provides an opinionated application structure and an integrated set of tools and APIs for building complete web applications. Q3. Why do we need Angular when we already have JavaScript? Expected Answer: JavaScript provides the programming language and browser APIs, but a large application also needs consistent ways to organize UI, navigation, forms, data access, dependency management, testing, and application state. Angular provides conventions and built in capabilities for these application level problems. Q4. What can we build with Angular? Expected Answer: Angular can be used to build single page applications, dashboards, enterprise applications, admin portals, e commerce applications, learning platforms, and other complex browser based applications. Q5. What is a Single Page Application (SPA)? Expected Answer: A SPA is a web application where the browser initially loads an application and then updates the displayed UI as the user navigates or interacts with it, instead of performing a full browser page reload for every application route. Q6. What is the role of Angular in an SPA? Expected Answer: Angular manages the application UI and its behavior in the browser. It provides components, templates, routing, services, forms, HTTP integration, and other application capabilities needed to build the SPA. Level 2 — Understanding Q7. What problems does Angular solve? Expected Answer: Angular helps solve common large application problems such as: Organizing UI into components Managing templates and user interaction Navigating between application views Sharing business logic through services Managing dependencies through dependency injection Handling forms and validation Communicating with backend APIs Testing application behavior Maintaining consistent project structure Q8. What is a component in Angular? Expected Answer: A component is a primary building block of an Angular application's UI. It combines a template, application logic, and styling to represent a part of the user interface. Q9. What is the relationship between Angular and TypeScript? Expected Answer: Angular is built with TypeScript and provides first class TypeScript support. TypeScript adds static typing and other language features that help developers build and maintain large applications. Q10. Does Angular replace HTML, CSS, and JavaScript? Expected Answer: No. Angular works with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript/TypeScript. It provides a framework and additional APIs for structuring and managing an application. Q11. What is Angular CLI? Expected Answer: Angular CLI is the command line tool used to create, develop, test, build, and maintain Angular applications. For example, it can create a new application and generate Angular artifacts. Q12. Who develops Angular? Expected Answer: Angular is developed and maintained by Google together with its open source community. Level 3 — Comparison Questions Q13. Angular vs plain JavaScript — what is the difference? Expected Answer: Plain JavaScript gives developers direct control over browser behavior and application code, but the developer must decide how to structure a large application. Angular provides an application framework with conventions and built in capabilities for common concerns. Q14. Angular vs React — what is the difference? Expected Answer: Angular is a full frontend framework with an integrated set of application capabilities. React is primarily a UI library, and applications commonly add additional libraries or frameworks for concerns such as routing and state management. Both can be used to build large web applications. Q15. Why might a team choose Angular for an enterprise application? Expected Answer: A team may choose Angular when it values an integrated framework, consistent application patterns, TypeScript support, dependency injection, built in routing/forms/HTTP capabilities, and long term maintainability across a large team. Level 4 — Scenario Questions Q16. You are asked to build a large job portal. Why might you choose Angular? Expected Answer: I would evaluate the project requirements first. If the application needs a structured architecture, many reusable components, routing, forms, API integration, authentication, testing, and a large development team, Angular's integrated framework and conventions can provide a consistent foundation. Q17. Your team has many developers working on the same frontend. What Angular features can help? Expected Answer: Angular's component architecture, dependency injection, routing, TypeScript support, CLI tooling, conventions, testing tools, and modular feature boundaries can help teams maintain consistency and separation of responsibilities. Q18. A beginner says, "Angular is only for creating HTML pages." How would you explain it? Expected Answer: Angular does much more than render HTML. It provides a complete application framework for managing UI, user interaction, navigation, services, dependencies, forms, API communication, application state, testing, and other concerns. Level 5 — Interviewer Follow Up Questions Be prepared for these follow ups: Why is Angular called a framework? Why does Angular use TypeScript? What is a component? What is an SPA? What is Angular CLI used for? What are the major building blocks of Angular? When would you choose Angular instead of plain JavaScript? When would you choose Angular instead of React? Is Angular suitable only for large applications? What does "opinionated framework" mean? What makes Angular suitable for team development? Coding / Practical Question Q19. Create a simple Angular application and explain its architecture. The learner should be able to identify: Then explain what happens when the application starts at a high level. Debugging Scenario Q20. A developer says, "I can build the entire application with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, so Angular is unnecessary." How would you respond in an interview? Expected Answer: That is technically possible. The decision depends on application complexity and team requirements. For a small page, plain JavaScript may be sufficient. Property binding vs attribute binding? Expected Answer: Property binding updates a DOM property; attribute binding updates an HTML attribute. For example, [disabled] is a property binding while [attr.aria label] is attribute binding. 3. How do you conditionally apply one class? Expected Answer: Use [class.className] with a boolean expression. 4. How do you bind a style value? Expected Answer: Use bindings such as [style.color] or [style.width.px] for dynamic style values. 5. How do you bind multiple classes? Expected Answer: ARIA values are HTML attributes, so [attr.aria label] and similar bindings are appropriate. 7. What happens when an attribute binding evaluates to null? Expected Answer: Angular removes the attribute, which is useful for optional attributes. 8. When should classes be preferred over inline styles? Expected Answer: Prefer classes for reusable visual states; use styles for genuinely dynamic values. 9. JobHub scenario: mark urgent jobs visually. How? text: Day 19 Interview Questions — @empty, track and Efficient Lists Interview Goal Be able to explain @empty, track and Efficient Lists , write the relevant Angular code, discuss trade offs, and apply it to a realistic JobHub feature. Interview Questions 1. What is @empty? Expected Answer: It renders fallback UI when an @for collection contains no items. 2. Why is an empty state different from loading? Expected Answer: Empty means the request completed with no items; loading means data is still being obtained. 3. Why should loading be explicit? Expected Answer: Otherwise an initial empty array can incorrectly display an empty result message while the request is still running. 4. Why does track matter during refresh? Expected Answer: It lets Angular match incoming items to existing DOM nodes by stable identity. 5. Why is tracking by index risky for dynamic lists? Expected Answer: Insertion, deletion, and reordering can change indexes even when the underlying item is the same. 6. What makes list rendering expensive? Expected Answer: Large DOM trees, repeated calculations, unnecessary child updates, and unstable identities. 7. How should a job list model loading, empty, error, and success? Expected Answer: Use explicit state; render the successful collection with @for and provide @empty for the completed empty result. 8. When should virtualization be considered? Expected Answer: When measurement shows that rendering a very large number of DOM items is a bottleneck. 9. JobHub scenario: recruiter data refreshes frequently. What should you inspect? Expected Answer: Stable tracking, state churn, request lifecycle, child updates, and measured rendering cost. Interviewer Follow Ups Why did you choose this approach? Interview Questions 1. What are common UI states in an Angular feature? Expected Answer: Typical states include loading, success, empty, and error; some features also need refreshing, disabled, or unauthorized states. 2. Why should UI states be explicit? Expected Answer: Explicit state prevents ambiguous conditions such as treating an empty array as both loading and completed empty. 3. How can modern control flow represent UI states? Expected Answer: Use @if, @else if, @else, @for, @empty, and @switch to make rendering branches clear. 4. Should loading state be inferred from data length? Expected Answer: No. A collection can be empty while loaded, so loading should be modeled separately. 5. How would you model a feature with several mutually exclusive states? Expected Answer: Use a typed state model or discriminated union when appropriate, then render each state explicitly. 6. What is the benefit of a discriminated union for UI state? Expected Answer: It makes valid states explicit and lets TypeScript help prevent impossible combinations. 7. How should error recovery be handled? Expected Answer: Show actionable error UI and connect retry to the appropriate data access operation. 8. How would JobHub distinguish empty search results from an API failure? Expected Answer: Use separate success empty and error states instead of deriving both from the jobs array. 9. What is a common UI state anti pattern? Expected Answer: A collection of unrelated booleans that can accidentally represent contradictory states. Interviewer Follow Ups Why did you choose this approach? text: Day 41 Interview Questions — Why Directives and Pipes? Interview Goal Explain Why Directives and Pipes? , implement the relevant Angular pattern, discuss trade offs, and apply it to a realistic JobHub scenario. Interview Questions 1. What is a directive in Angular? Expected Answer: A directive adds reusable behavior to an existing host element or component without owning a new piece of UI structure. 2. What is the difference between a component and a directive? Expected Answer: A component owns its own template and UI structure; a directive attaches to an existing host element and enhances it. 3. What is a pipe used for? Expected Answer: A pipe transforms a value for display in a template, such as formatting a date or currency amount. 4. Why should display formatting live in a pipe rather than inside a component method? Expected Answer: Keeping formatting in a pipe keeps templates declarative and reusable, and separates presentation from component logic. 5. Why not just create a component for every reusable behavior? Expected Answer: Creating a component for simple shared behavior can be unnecessary overhead; a directive can add behavior without owning surrounding markup. 6. Give an example of something that is naturally a directive rather than a component. Expected Answer: A reusable highlight on hover behavior applied to buttons, cards, or inputs. 7. Give an example of something that is naturally a pipe. Expected Answer: Formatting a salary number as currency or a date as a readable string. 8. What is a common mistake when deciding between a component, directive, or pipe? Expected Answer: Putting business calculations inside presentation pipes, or using a pipe to mutate application state. 9. JobHub scenario: JobHub needs a reusable hover highlight behavior on job cards and a way to format salary numbers for display. Which abstractions fit each requirement? Expected Answer: The hover highlight behavior fits a directive because it enhances existing host elements; the salary formatting fits a pipe because it is a display transformation. text: Day 47 Interview Questions — Custom Pipes Interview Goal Explain Custom Pipes , implement the relevant Angular pattern, discuss trade offs, and apply it to a realistic JobHub scenario. Interview Questions 1. When should you create a custom pipe instead of using a built in one? Expected Answer: When the required display transformation is not covered by a built in pipe, such as a domain specific relative time or label format. 2. What is a pure pipe? Expected Answer: A pipe that is recalculated only when Angular detects that its input reference or primitive value has changed. 3. When is an impure pipe justified, and what is the risk of using one? Expected Answer: It is justified only for rare cases needing recalculation on every change detection cycle; the risk is unnecessary recalculation and performance cost. 4. What should a custom pipe never do? Expected Answer: Make API calls, mutate external state, or produce non deterministic output for the same input. 5. How would you implement a relativeDays pipe that shows "today", "1 day ago", "5 days ago"? Expected Answer: Implement a method that returns "today" for 0, "1 day ago" for 1, and otherwise. 6. Why keep a custom pipe's transform() method deterministic? Expected Answer: Deterministic output for the same input lets Angular safely treat the pipe as pure and makes behavior predictable and testable. 7. What is a common mistake when writing custom pipes? Expected Answer: Putting API calls or state mutation inside a pipe instead of keeping it a pure presentation transformation. 8. JobHub scenario: JobHub wants to show "Posted 3 days ago" from a postedDaysAgo number. Where should the formatting rule live and why? Expected Answer: In a custom relativeDays pipe, so the presentation rule stays out of the template and out of business components and can be reused anywhere it is needed. text: Day 48 Interview Questions — Directive and Pipe Design Patterns Interview Goal Explain Directive and Pipe Design Patterns , implement the relevant Angular pattern, discuss trade offs, and apply it to a realistic JobHub scenario. Interview Questions 1. How do you decide between a component, a directive, and a pipe for a given requirement? Expected Answer: Use a component when you own UI structure, a directive when you enhance an existing host element with reusable behavior, and a pipe when you transform a value for display. 2. What are the traits of a well designed directive or pipe? Expected Answer: One clear responsibility, a small public API, predictable behavior, no unnecessary global dependencies, and easy testability. 3. When should logic remain a plain TypeScript function instead of becoming a directive or pipe? Expected Answer: When it has no template binding or host behavior need and is simpler as an ordinary reusable function. 4. Why should you avoid expensive computations inside templates or pipes? Expected Answer: Presentation transformations run as part of rendering, so expensive repeated calculations can hurt rendering performance. 5. What should you do if a transformation is expensive or business critical rather than hiding it in a pipe? Expected Answer: Compute and own the value where it belongs (such as a service or component state) instead of relying on a pipe to solve the performance or ownership problem. 6. What is over abstraction with directives and pipes, and why is it a problem? Expected Answer: Creating unnecessary directives or pipes for logic that does not need reuse, which adds indirection and complexity without real benefit. 7. What is a common mistake when refactoring logic into directives and pipes? Expected Answer: Extracting an abstraction that does not have a genuine reuse need, or mixing business logic into what should be a presentation only directive or pipe. 8. JobHub scenario: reviewing ten pieces of UI logic in the Job Portal, how would you classify each as component, directive, pipe, function, or service? Expected Answer: Classify by asking whether it owns UI structure (component), enhances a host element (directive), transforms a display value (pipe), needs no template binding (function), or owns shared state/behavior (service). Interviewer Follow Ups Why did you choose this approach? What alternative Angular approach could solve the same problem? What happens when the data changes? How would you test this behavior? What would you change for a large enterprise application? Common Interview Trap Do not memorize syntax alone. Explain why the pattern fits the problem and which layer owns the responsibility. text: Day 50 Interview Questions — Why Component Composition? Interview Goal Explain Why Component Composition? , implement the relevant Angular pattern, discuss trade offs, and apply it to a realistic JobHub scenario. Interview Questions 1. What is component composition? Expected Answer: It builds a larger UI by combining focused components rather than putting all UI behavior into one component. 2. Why is composition important in Angular? Expected Answer: It improves reuse, separation of responsibilities, testability, and maintainability. 3. What is the difference between composition and inheritance for UI? Expected Answer: Composition combines components through contracts and structure; inheritance creates tighter class relationships and is usually not the primary UI reuse mechanism. 4. What makes a component composable? Expected Answer: A clear API, focused responsibility, predictable inputs/outputs, and flexible content or child composition. 5. How does content projection support composition? Expected Answer: A reusable component can provide structure while consumers supply content through ng content. 6. When should a component be split into smaller components? Expected Answer: When a section has a distinct responsibility, repeated UI pattern, independent state, or a useful reusable contract. 7. What is over componentization? Expected Answer: Splitting UI into many tiny components without meaningful boundaries, which can increase complexity and communication overhead. 8. How should a reusable component avoid domain coupling? Expected Answer: Expose generic typed UI contracts and keep feature specific orchestration outside the reusable component. 9. JobHub scenario: a dashboard contains header, filters, job list, job card, and actions. How would you compose it? Expected Answer: Use focused components with explicit contracts, letting the feature/container coordinate data and actions while reusable UI components stay domain light. Interviewer Follow Ups Why did you choose this component boundary? What alternative design could solve the same problem? Who owns the state? How would you test the composition? What would you change for a large enterprise application? Common Interview Trap Do not split components merely to make files smaller. A component should have a meaningful responsibility and a clear contract. Self Assessment [ ] I can explain the concept without documentation. [ ] I can design a small component hierarchy. text: Day 61 Interview Questions — Provider Scope and Service Lifetimes Interview Goal Understand Angular's injector hierarchy, provider scope, service instance sharing, and how lifetime decisions affect application architecture. Interview Questions 1. What is an Angular injector? Expected Answer: An injector resolves dependencies and creates or retrieves the instances requested by Angular components, services, routes, and other injectable consumers. 2. What does generally mean? Expected Answer: The service is registered with the root injector and is normally shared across the application. 3. Why would you use a component level provider? Expected Answer: To create a dependency instance scoped to that component's injector rather than sharing the root instance. 4. What is the practical effect of provider scope? Expected Answer: It determines which consumers can resolve a dependency from that injector hierarchy and how instances are shared. 5. Can two components have separate service instances? Expected Answer: Yes, if the service is provided in each component's injector scope. 6. Why does service lifetime matter? Expected Answer: It affects state sharing, resource ownership, cleanup, and whether multiple consumers see the same instance. 7. What is a common provider scope mistake? Expected Answer: Using root scope for state that should be isolated to a feature or component. 8. How would you decide service scope? Expected Answer: Start from state or resource ownership: application wide services can be root scoped, while isolated feature or component state can use narrower providers. 9. JobHub scenario: each JobEditor should maintain independent draft state. What scope fits? Expected Answer: Provide the draft state service at the appropriate editor or feature boundary so each editor gets its own instance. Interviewer Follow Ups Why did you choose this provider scope? What happens if the service is moved to root? How would you test instance isolation? How does provider scope affect state ownership? What would you choose for an enterprise feature? Common Interview Trap Do not assume every service should be provided in root. Choose scope based on ownership and intended sharing. Self Assessment [ ] I can explain injector hierarchy. text: Day 69 Interview Questions — Why Component Lifecycle Matters Interview Goal Understand Angular component lifecycle stages and place setup, rendering work, reactions, and cleanup appropriately. Expected Answer: Reactive dependencies can reduce manual synchronization while lifecycle APIs remain useful for setup, DOM access, and cleanup. 6. What is a common lifecycle anti pattern? Expected Answer: Putting unrelated business logic into hooks simply because those hooks execute during the lifecycle. 7. JobHub scenario Expected Answer: If JobDetails starts polling, the polling resource must be stopped when the component is destroyed. Interviewer Follow Ups Which work belongs in initialization?
