Debugging Scenario The submit button remains enabled while a request is running, allowing duplicate submissions. Explain the state model you would introduce. Common Interview Traps Relying only on red borders. Hiding validation messages from assistive technologies. Treating client validation as security. Losing form values after failed submission. Project Connection — JobHub Good form UX is critical for job creation, applications, profile editing, and recruiter workflows. Quick Revision Production forms combine validation state, submission state, accessibility, feedback, and recovery behavior. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can explain not just how validation works, but how users experience validation.

title: Form Architecture and Reusable Patterns
text: Day 103 — Form Architecture and Reusable Patterns Interview Goal Design maintainable Angular forms instead of placing all form logic inside one component. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. What is form architecture? 2. Why should complex forms be broken into smaller sections? 3. When should form creation logic be extracted into a service or factory? 4. What is a reusable form component? 5. Why should validation rules have a clear ownership boundary? Level 2 — Understanding 1. Compare one large form component with section based form components. 2. Where should API mapping logic live? 3. How would you separate UI form models from backend DTOs? 4. When should a child component own a FormGroup) better than a CVA component? How would you test a reusable form section? Coding Question Design a typed that creates a create/edit Job form without duplicating control definitions. Debugging Scenario An edit screen patches API data directly into the form and later submits UI only fields back to the API. Identify the architectural problem. Common Interview Traps Coupling forms directly to backend DTOs. Duplicating validation logic. Creating giant reusable components. Mixing navigation, API, and UI responsibilities. Project Connection — JobHub JobHub should use reusable form sections while keeping feature specific orchestration inside candidate, recruiter, and admin features. Quick Revision Good form architecture separates form models, reusable controls, validation, API mapping, and feature orchestration. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can explain where each responsibility belongs in a complex Angular form.

title: Mini Project: Job Application Form
text: Day 104 — Mini Project: Job Application Form Interview Goal Apply Angular Forms concepts to a realistic job application workflow. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. What controls are needed for a job application form? 2. Which fields should be required? 3. Which validations belong on the client? 4. Which rules must also be enforced by the backend? 5. How should submission state be represented? Level 2 — Understanding 1. Why should resume validation not rely only on file extension? 2. How would you model optional versus required application fields? 3. How should draft and submitted states differ? 4. How would you prevent duplicate applications? 5. How would you represent API errors in the form? Level 3 — Practical 1. Build a typed application form. 2. Add experience, notice period, salary expectation, and resume fields. 3. Add a custom control using CVA. 4. Add cross field validation. 5. Add loading, success, failure, and retry states. Level 4 — JobHub Scenarios 1. A candidate applies twice because of a network retry. How should UI and backend cooperate? 2. Resume upload succeeds but application submission fails. How should the UI recover? 3. Backend returns a validation error for a field the client considers valid. How should the form handle it? 4. The form must support save as draft. What additional state is required? Level 5 — Interviewer Follow Ups Why is backend validation still required? How would you test the complete submission flow? How would you separate file upload from application submission? What would you log when submission fails? Coding Question Implement the application form with strict typing, validation, submission state, and API error handling. Debugging Scenario The form becomes permanently disabled after a failed submission. Identify the missing state transition. Common Interview Traps Assuming HTTP 200 means business success. Trusting client validation as security. Combining file upload and application submission into one untestable component. Forgetting retry and recovery UX. Project Connection — JobHub This is the final Forms module exercise and becomes the basis for later HTTP integration. Quick Revision A production form is a stateful workflow, not just a collection of inputs. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can explain the complete lifecycle from user input to validated submission and recovery.

title: Why HTTP & API Integration?
text: Day 105 — Why HTTP & API Integration? Interview Goal Understand why frontend applications need APIs and how Angular should interact with backend systems. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. What is HTTP? 2. What is an API? 3. Why does an Angular application need a backend API? 4. What is the difference between a client and a server? 5. What are GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE commonly used for? Level 2 — Understanding 1. Explain request, response, headers, body, and status code. 2. Why should API calls not be scattered throughout UI components? 3. What is the difference between transport models and UI models? 4. Why should HTTP errors be handled explicitly? 5. What does idempotency mean at a high level? Level 3 — Practical 1. Design API endpoints for JobHub jobs and applications. 2. Define TypeScript interfaces for request and response payloads. 3. Decide which operations should use GET, POST, PATCH, and DELETE. 4. Design loading, success, empty, and error states for an API backed page. 5. Explain frontend behavior when the network is unavailable. Level 4 — JobHub Scenarios 1. Job search needs filters, pagination, and sorting. What should the API contract contain? 2. A recruiter edits a job while two browser tabs contain the same record. What consistency concerns exist? 3. The jobs API returns fields the UI does not need. Should the component consume the raw response directly? 4. The API changes a field name. How can the frontend limit the impact? Level 5 — Interviewer Follow Ups Why use a data access service? What belongs in an API contract? How do HTTP status codes influence UI behavior? Where should request/response mapping happen? Coding Question Design a typed Job API contract for list, details, create, update, and delete operations. Debugging Scenario Five components each call the same jobs endpoint independently. Explain the architectural and performance problems this can create. Common Interview Traps Treating HTTP as only GET requests. Mixing API DTOs directly into every template. Ignoring cancellation and stale requests. Assuming network success means business success. Project Connection — JobHub HTTP integration turns JobHub from a local UI into a real application backed by services. Quick Revision A strong Angular API layer has clear contracts, typed models, centralized data access, explicit UI states, and error handling. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can design an API integration boundary before writing the component.

title: HttpClient and provideHttpClient
text: Day 106 — HttpClient and provideHttpClient Interview Goal Understand Angular's modern HTTP setup and how fits into dependency injection. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. What is Angular HttpClient provideHttpClient() HttpClient HttpClient inject(HttpClient) Observable HttpClient provideHttpClient() JobApiService inject(HttpClient) Observable<unknown provideHttpClient() JobApiService getJobs() createJob() inject(HttpClient) NullInjectorError HttpClient any provideHttpClient()), then consume it through injected typed services. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can explain both the configuration and architectural role of HttpClient.

title: GET Requests and Typed Responses
text: Day 107 — GET Requests and Typed Responses Interview Goal Build safe, typed GET requests and understand how response contracts affect Angular UI code. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. How do you make a GET request with HttpClient.get<T () T)? 3. When would you use JobListResponse null switchMap searchJobs(params) HttpParams response.items response.data`. Explain how a mapping boundary prevents this mismatch from spreading. Common Interview Traps Assuming TypeScript generics validate server JSON. Treating empty data as an error. Building query strings manually. Ignoring stale search responses. Project Connection — JobHub Typed GET APIs power job search, filtering, recruiter lists, and admin screens. Quick Revision Typed HTTP improves compile time safety, but runtime API data still needs trustworthy contracts or validation. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can explain both TypeScript typing and its limits.

title: POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE
text: Day 108 — POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE Interview Goal Understand how Angular sends mutation requests and how HTTP semantics influence application design. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. What is POST used for? 2. What is the typical purpose of PUT? 3. What is PATCH used for? 4. What is DELETE used for? 5. How do you send a request body with HttpClient? Level 2 — Understanding 1. Compare PUT and PATCH. 2. What does idempotent mean? 3. Why should create and update payloads often use different types? 4. Why should the UI not assume every successful mutation returns a full entity? 5. How should the frontend react to common mutation status codes? Level 3 — Practical 1. Implement create job with POST. 2. Implement full job replacement with PUT. 3. Implement partial job updates with PATCH. 4. Implement job deletion with DELETE. 5. Define separate create, update, and response models. Level 4 — JobHub Scenarios 1. Recruiters edit only salary and location. Would PATCH or PUT be appropriate based on the API contract? 2. Delete returns no body. How should the UI update local state? 3. Create returns a generated job ID. How should the UI use it? 4. PATCH succeeds but the local job list still shows old data. What synchronization strategies exist? Level 5 — Interviewer Follow Ups Is PUT always idempotent? Can POST be idempotent in practice? How would you handle optimistic versus server confirmed UI updates? Where should mutation errors become user facing messages? Coding Question Create a typed with create, update, partial update, and delete methods. Debugging Scenario A PATCH method sends the complete UI object including read only fields and the backend rejects it. Identify the contract problem. Common Interview Traps Treating PUT and PATCH as interchangeable. Reusing one type for every API operation. Assuming success always returns an entity. Updating UI optimistically without a recovery strategy. Project Connection — JobHub Recruiter job management depends on reliable create, update, and delete API flows. Quick Revision HTTP method semantics should match the backend contract; request and response types should reflect each operation. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can choose and implement mutation methods based on API semantics rather than habit.

title: Request Parameters, Headers and Options
text: Day 109 — Request Parameters, Headers and Options Interview Goal Understand how to control Angular HTTP requests without leaking transport details into UI components. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. What are query parameters? 2. What are HTTP headers? 3. What is a request body? 4. What is the purpose of request options in HttpClient? 5. Why should headers and parameters be built deliberately? Level 2 — Understanding 1. Compare query parameters, headers, and request body. 2. When would you use HttpHeaders)? 4. Why might a request need credentials or a specific response type? 5. What should be centralized in an interceptor instead of repeated in every service? Level 3 — Practical 1. Build typed query parameters for job filtering. 2. Add an header where the API contract requires it. 3. Add correlation/request metadata through an appropriate interceptor strategy. 4. Use request options for non default response handling when required. 5. Keep feature services independent of low level authentication header construction. Level 4 — JobHub Scenarios 1. Every authenticated API request needs the same access token. Where should that concern live? 2. Job search supports optional filters. How do you avoid meaningless empty parameters? 3. A file download requires a binary response. How does that differ from a normal JSON request? 4. A backend requires a tenant or organization identifier. Would you put it in the URL, header, or body? Explain based on the API contract. Level 5 — Interviewer Follow Ups What are the risks of manually duplicating authorization headers? What belongs in an interceptor versus a feature API service? How do you test request headers and query parameters? Can request headers be trusted for authorization? Coding Question Implement a typed search request with optional filters and query parameters, keeping transport construction inside the API service. Debugging Scenario A request sends and when filters are empty. Explain how you would construct parameters cleanly. Common Interview Traps Putting authorization logic in every component. Confusing headers with secure authorization decisions. Manually concatenating URLs. Sending UI only values as API parameters. Project Connection — JobHub Clean request construction becomes important as JobHub adds filtering, authentication, multi tenant data, uploads, and downloads. Quick Revision Parameters describe query selection, headers describe request metadata, and bodies carry operation data according to the API contract. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can design request options without coupling UI code to HTTP transport details.

title: Loading, Success, Empty and Error States
text: Day 110 — Loading, Success, Empty and Error States Interview Goal Design API backed Angular screens around explicit asynchronous UI states. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. Why is loading state necessary? 2. What is the difference between empty and error state? 3. Why should an API backed screen not assume data is immediately available? 4. What should happen while a mutation request is running? 5. Why should users have a recovery action after recoverable failures? Level 2 — Understanding 1. Model loading, success, empty, and error as explicit states. 2. Why is a single boolean such as often insufficient for complex screens? 3. How should initial loading differ from background refresh? 4. How should retry behavior work? 5. Why should stale data sometimes remain visible during refresh? Level 3 — Practical 1. Build a job list state model with loading, data, empty, and error states. 2. Add a retry action. 3. Add a skeleton for initial loading. 4. Show a non blocking refresh state when cached data exists. 5. Prevent duplicate mutation submissions. Level 4 — JobHub Scenarios 1. Job search initially loads 20 jobs, then refresh fails. Should existing jobs disappear? 2. The API returns HTTP 200 with zero jobs. How should UI distinguish this from failure? 3. A job details request fails after navigation. What should the page show? 4. A recruiter saves a job successfully but the notification fails. Which operation is successful? Level 5 — Interviewer Follow Ups Would you model status as a union type? When should stale data be retained? How would signals represent asynchronous UI state? How would you test each state independently? Coding Question Create a typed using a discriminated union such as and render each state with Angular control flow. Debugging Scenario A screen shows a blank page during API failure because the template only handles success. Explain the missing state transition. Common Interview Traps Treating empty as error. Hiding recoverable errors. Replacing useful stale data with a blank loading screen. Using unrelated booleans that allow impossible states. Project Connection — JobHub This state model becomes the foundation for later HTTP error handling, signals, RxJS, and state management modules. Quick Revision Explicit asynchronous states make API backed UIs predictable, testable, and resilient. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can model API state without creating contradictory combinations of flags.

title: HttpClient Services and API Boundaries
text: Day 111 — HttpClient Services and API Boundaries Interview Goal Design a clean data access boundary between Angular features and backend APIs. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. Why create an API service instead of calling HttpClient directly from components? 2. What responsibility should a data access service own? 3. What is an API boundary? 4. Why should components avoid knowing URL construction details? 5. What is the benefit of typed service methods? Level 2 — Understanding 1. Compare a component that calls HttpClient directly with one that uses JobApiService. 2. Where should request and response mapping happen? 3. Should an API service expose raw HttpClient objects or feature oriented methods? 4. How does a service boundary improve testing? 5. When should a feature have more than one data access service? Level 3 — Practical 1. Create a typed JobApiService. 2. Separate list, detail, create, update, and delete methods. 3. Keep endpoint paths centralized. 4. Map API DTOs to UI models. 5. Define a service contract that can be mocked in tests. JobHub Scenarios 1. Candidate and recruiter screens use different job operations. How would you structure the API boundary? 2. Backend DTO names differ from UI model names. Where should mapping occur? 3. Three features need the same endpoint. How do you avoid duplicated transport logic? 4. A backend endpoint changes. How can the service boundary reduce UI changes? Interviewer Follow Ups What is the difference between a service and a facade? Should API services contain business rules? How would you mock the API boundary? How would you prevent an API service from becoming a giant class? Coding Question Design a typed JobApiService with separate methods for job search, details, create, update, and delete. Debugging Scenario A component contains URL strings, HttpParams construction, DTO mapping, notifications, and navigation. Identify the violated boundaries. Common Interview Traps Treating services as dumping grounds. Returning backend DTOs everywhere. Mixing navigation with data access. Hiding business rules inside transport code. Project Connection — JobHub The API boundary becomes the foundation for later interceptors, authentication, state management, and testing. Quick Revision Feature code should depend on clear data access contracts rather than raw HTTP transport details. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can explain where API transport ends and feature behavior begins.

title: API Models to UI Models
text: Day 112 — API Models to UI Models Interview Goal Learn why backend DTOs and frontend UI models should sometimes remain separate. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. What is a DTO? 2. What is a UI model? 3. Why might the two models differ? 4. What is data mapping? 5. Where should mapping logic live? Level 2 — Understanding 1. What problems occur when backend DTOs are used directly in templates? 2. Why might an API use snake case while a UI uses camelCase? 3. How should nullable API fields be represented? 4. Why should read only API fields not automatically become editable form fields? 5. What is the cost of adding a mapping layer? Level 3 — Practical 1. Create JobApiResponse and Job UI models. 2. Map API dates into a UI friendly representation. 3. Map backend status codes into UI states. 4. Map nested API objects into view models. 5. Map form values into create/update API payloads. JobHub Scenarios 1. API returns , while UI expects . Where should conversion happen? 2. API returns internal status codes that should not appear in the UI. How would you model them? 3. Backend adds fields that the UI does not need. Should the UI model change? 4. The same API job is displayed differently in candidate and recruiter screens. Would you use one UI model? Interviewer Follow Ups When is a mapping layer unnecessary? How do mapping functions affect performance? How would you test mappings? Should mapping happen in the API service or a separate mapper? Coding Question Create typed mapping functions for API Job DTO → CandidateJob and CandidateJobForm → CreateJobRequest. Debugging Scenario A backend rename forces changes across 20 templates. Explain how a mapping boundary could have limited the impact. Common Interview Traps Assuming API models are always ideal UI models. Hiding mapping logic inside templates. Converting data repeatedly in multiple components. Ignoring nullability. Project Connection — JobHub Model separation protects the UI from backend contract changes and supports different candidate/recruiter views. Quick Revision API models describe transport contracts; UI models describe what the frontend needs. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can justify model separation based on actual boundary differences rather than creating abstraction for its own sake.

title: HTTP Interceptors
text: Day 113 — HTTP Interceptors Interview Goal Understand how Angular HTTP interceptors centralize cross cutting request and response behavior. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. What is an HTTP interceptor? 2. Why would an application use an interceptor? 3. What is the difference between request and response interception? 4. How are interceptors configured in a standalone Angular application? 5. Can an interceptor modify a request? Level 2 — Understanding 1. Explain the interceptor chain. 2. Why should authorization headers usually be centralized? 3. How can an interceptor add correlation IDs? 4. What should an interceptor avoid doing? 5. How can multiple interceptors work together? Level 3 — Practical 1. Create a functional interceptor. 2. Add an authorization header when appropriate. 3. Add request logging for development diagnostics. 4. Add a correlation/request ID. 5. Handle a common response or transport error consistently. JobHub Scenarios 1. Every protected API request needs authentication metadata. Where should it be added? 2. Public job search endpoints must not receive protected session headers. How would the interceptor decide? 3. A logging interceptor exposes sensitive data. What should change? 4. Two interceptors modify the same header. How would you reason about ordering and ownership? Interviewer Follow Ups What is a functional interceptor? What is the difference between interceptors and API services? Can interceptors implement business logic? How would you test an interceptor? Coding Question Implement an interceptor that conditionally adds an authentication header while preserving the immutable request model. Debugging Scenario A token header is added twice. Identify possible interceptor registration or cloning problems. Common Interview Traps Treating interceptors as global business logic. Logging tokens or sensitive payloads. Mutating requests instead of cloning them. Applying auth headers to every request without considering public endpoints. Project Connection — JobHub Interceptors provide the platform level HTTP pipeline for authentication, diagnostics, and consistent transport behavior. Quick Revision Interceptors are best for cross cutting HTTP concerns, not feature specific business behavior. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can explain why a concern belongs in an interceptor instead of an API service or component.

title: Authentication Headers and Request Context
text: Day 114 — Authentication Headers and Request Context Interview Goal Understand how authentication metadata and request specific context can be carried through Angular HTTP requests. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. Why do protected APIs require authentication information? 2. What is an authorization header? 3. What is request context? 4. Why should authentication logic not be duplicated in every API service? 5. What is the difference between authentication metadata and business data? Level 2 — Understanding 1. When should an auth interceptor add credentials? 2. Why might some requests need to opt out of authentication? 3. What information should not be placed in query parameters? 4. How can request context help an interceptor make a decision? 5. Why must the backend remain authoritative for authorization? Level 3 — Practical 1. Design an authenticated request flow. 2. Mark selected requests as public. 3. Use request context for interceptor behavior where appropriate. 4. Keep feature services independent of token construction. 5. Design an API contract for authenticated job operations. JobHub Scenarios 1. Job search is public but applying requires authentication. How should the HTTP layer distinguish them? 2. A recruiter endpoint requires a special permission. Should the frontend decide whether the user is authorized? 3. A request must skip a retry policy. How could request context represent that requirement? 4. Multiple APIs have different authentication requirements. How would you avoid hard coded checks everywhere? Interviewer Follow Ups What is HttpContext used for? Can a request context value itself authorize a user? Where should role and permission enforcement occur? How would you test context driven interceptor behavior? Coding Question Design a request option using Angular HTTP context to mark an endpoint as public. Debugging Scenario A public endpoint receives an authentication header and fails through an upstream gateway. Identify where the policy should be adjusted. Common Interview Traps Treating request context as a security boundary. Putting authorization decisions only in the UI. Sending sensitive information through URLs. Hard coding endpoint checks in many services. Project Connection — JobHub Request context helps coordinate cross cutting transport policies while backend authorization remains authoritative. Quick Revision Frontend request metadata can influence transport behavior, but it must never replace server side authorization.

title: HTTP Error Handling and Retry
text: Day 115 — HTTP Error Handling and Retry Interview Goal Handle transport failures and retries without creating duplicate actions or poor user experiences. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. What is an HTTP error? 2. What is the difference between client side and server side failure? 3. What does retry mean? 4. Why should every failed request not be retried automatically? 5. What is the purpose of a user facing retry action? Level 2 — Understanding 1. Which failures may be appropriate for automatic retry? 2. Why can retrying POST requests be dangerous? 3. How should timeout like failures be represented to users? 4. What is exponential backoff conceptually? 5. Where should common transport error handling live? Level 3 — Practical 1. Add explicit error handling to an API service. 2. Retry a suitable transient GET request with a bounded policy. 3. Avoid retrying non idempotent mutations blindly. 4. Map HTTP errors into UI friendly error states. 5. Add a manual retry action. JobHub Scenarios 1. Job search temporarily fails due to a network interruption. Would you retry automatically? 2. Application submission returns an unknown server error. Should the frontend automatically resubmit? 3. A user clicks Retry five times. How should the UI protect the user and backend? 4. Backend returns 429. What should the application consider? Interviewer Follow Ups What is exponential backoff? How do idempotency and retry relate? Should error messages expose raw backend responses? How would you test retry behavior? Coding Question Implement bounded retry handling for a read only jobs request and expose a final error state. Debugging Scenario A POST request creates duplicate applications after automatic retry. Explain the failure and safer design. Common Interview Traps Retrying every request. Infinite retry loops. Treating every 4xx as transient. Showing raw backend exception text to users. Project Connection — JobHub Reliable job search and application workflows require deliberate error and retry policies. Quick Revision Retry is a resilience strategy, not a default response to every error. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can choose retry behavior based on request semantics and failure type.

title: httpResource()
text: Day 116 — httpResource() Interview Goal Understand Angular's signal oriented HTTP resource API and when it may simplify reactive data fetching. Version Note is version sensitive. Verify the Angular version and API status before using it in production code. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. What problem does address? 2. How is a resource oriented API different from manually subscribing to HttpClient? 3. How does it relate to Angular Signals? 4. What kinds of state can a resource expose? 5. Why should experimental APIs be isolated carefully? Level 2 — Understanding 1. Compare with a traditional HttpClient service. 2. How can reactive request parameters trigger data refresh? 3. How should loading and error states be represented? 4. What are the trade offs of adopting a version sensitive API? 5. When would a normal HttpClient service still be preferable? Level 3 — Practical 1. Build a small read only job search example using the resource API where supported. 2. Connect reactive search parameters to the request. 3. Render loading, value, and error states. 4. Keep mutation operations in an appropriate API service. 5. Document the Angular version requirement. JobHub Scenarios 1. Candidate search should update when filters change. Would a resource abstraction help? 2. The team supports multiple Angular versions. What adoption risk exists? 3. A resource API changes between Angular releases. How would you isolate migration work? 4. A complex workflow has multiple dependent mutations. Would resource APIs be the only abstraction? Interviewer Follow Ups Is the same as HttpClient? When should an experimental API be avoided? How would you test resource driven UI state? How would you migrate away if the API changed? Coding Question Create a version aware example showing a reactive read only job search with explicit loading and error states. Debugging Scenario A project upgrades Angular and the resource API example no longer matches the installed API. Explain how version sensitive documentation should be handled. Common Interview Traps Presenting experimental APIs as universally stable. Replacing every HttpClient call with resources. Ignoring supported version constraints. Mixing experimental and production architecture without boundaries. Project Connection — JobHub This topic introduces modern signal oriented data fetching while preserving a conventional HttpClient foundation. Quick Revision Use version sensitive Angular APIs deliberately and keep production architecture easy to migrate. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can explain both the benefit and adoption risk of .

title: API Configuration
text: Day 117 — API Configuration Interview Goal Design environment aware API configuration without scattering URLs and secrets through Angular code. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. Why should API URLs be configurable? 2. What is environment specific configuration? 3. Why should secrets not be stored in frontend source code? 4. What is runtime configuration? 5. Where should a feature obtain its API base URL? Level 2 — Understanding 1. Compare build time and runtime configuration. 2. Why is a frontend environment file not a secret store? 3. How can dependency injection provide configuration? 4. Why is hard coded URL construction difficult to maintain? 5. What should happen when required configuration is missing? Level 3 — Practical 1. Define a typed API configuration object. 2. Provide it through Angular dependency injection. 3. Support development and production API endpoints. 4. Validate required configuration at startup. 5. Keep API services independent of deployment specific values. JobHub Scenarios 1. JobHub runs locally, in test, staging, and production. How should the API base URL change? 2. A deployment platform injects runtime configuration. How can Angular consume it? 3. A developer puts a private API key in environment.ts. What is wrong? 4. A remote micro frontend needs a backend URL. How should configuration be coordinated? Interviewer Follow Ups What is an InjectionToken useful for? Why is runtime configuration valuable for containerized deployments? Can a frontend hide a secret? How would you test missing configuration? Coding Question Create a typed InjectionToken and inject it into a JobApiService. Debugging Scenario Production calls localhost because a URL was hard coded in a service. Explain the configuration boundary that was missed. Common Interview Traps Calling frontend configuration secrets. Hard coding production URLs. Mixing configuration with business logic. Assuming build time configuration covers every deployment model. Project Connection — JobHub Configuration strategy prepares JobHub for CI/CD, runtime deployment, and later micro frontend environments. Quick Revision Configuration belongs at application boundaries; secrets must remain server side.

title: API Architecture and Data Access
text: Day 118 — API Architecture and Data Access Interview Goal Combine HTTP knowledge into a maintainable Angular data access architecture. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. What is a data access layer? 2. Why separate API access from UI components? 3. What is the difference between API service and state service? 4. Why are request and response models important? 5. What is a facade in application architecture? Level 2 — Understanding 1. Describe the flow from component to API and back. 2. Where should caching decisions live? 3. Where should DTO mapping occur? 4. How should errors cross the data access boundary? 5. When does a feature need a facade between components and API services? Level 3 — Practical 1. Design a JobHub data access folder. 2. Separate API contracts, API services, mappers, and feature state. 3. Add a facade for a complex job search feature. 4. Define clear dependencies between UI and data access. 5. Design tests for each boundary. JobHub Scenarios 1. Job search, saved jobs, and job details all share job data. How would you prevent duplicated data logic? 2. Recruiter and candidate APIs expose different capabilities. How should boundaries reflect that? 3. A component directly manipulates API DTOs and local state. What would you refactor? 4. A data access service starts containing UI notifications and navigation. Where should those responsibilities move? Interviewer Follow Ups Service versus facade? API model versus domain model? Where should caching live? How do you keep a data access layer from becoming over engineered? Coding Question Sketch a JobHub data access architecture with API services, models, mappers, and an optional facade. Debugging Scenario A small API change requires edits across components, templates, and state stores. Identify missing boundaries. Common Interview Traps One giant API service. One model for transport, domain, and UI. Putting UI side effects in data access code. Adding abstraction without a real boundary. Project Connection — JobHub This architecture is reused in the later state management and enterprise architecture modules. Quick Revision Good data access creates explicit boundaries between transport, domain data, state, and presentation. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can draw the data flow and explain the ownership of each layer.

title: Mini Project: Job Search API Dashboard
text: Day 119 — Mini Project: Job Search API Dashboard Interview Goal Build a realistic API backed job search experience using typed HTTP architecture. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. What API operations does the dashboard need? 2. Which state should the UI represent? 3. Which filters belong in query parameters? 4. What should happen when there are no jobs? 5. What should happen when the API fails? Level 2 — Understanding 1. How would you model pagination? 2. How would you prevent stale search responses? 3. Where should API to UI mapping occur? 4. Where should loading and error state live? 5. How would you test the dashboard without a real backend? Level 3 — Practical 1. Create a typed JobApiService. 2. Implement search with filters and pagination. 3. Add loading, empty, success, and error states. 4. Add retry behavior. 5. Map API models to UI models. 6. Keep the component independent from URL construction. JobHub Scenarios 1. Search filters change rapidly while requests are in flight. How should the UI handle them? 2. The backend returns a page with no jobs but indicates more pages are unavailable. What state should render? 3. A refresh fails while old jobs are visible. How should the screen behave? 4. The API contract changes from to . Which layer should change? Interviewer Follow Ups Why use an API service? Why use typed models? Where would you add an interceptor? How would you test loading, empty, success, and error states? Coding Question Implement the core architecture for the Job Search API Dashboard using strict TypeScript and modern Angular control flow. Debugging Scenario The dashboard makes duplicate requests and occasionally displays stale results. Identify possible causes in request triggering and async coordination. Common Interview Traps Calling APIs directly from templates. Using untyped response data. Treating empty as error. Ignoring stale request handling. Project Connection — JobHub This mini project closes the first HTTP block and prepares the learner for advanced HTTP, authentication, and state management. Quick Revision A production API dashboard combines typed contracts, data access boundaries, explicit async state, and resilient request handling. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can design the data flow before implementing the screen.

title: Why Authentication & Authorization?
text: Day 120 — Why Authentication & Authorization? Interview Goal Understand the difference between authentication and authorization and how they shape an Angular application's security architecture. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. What is authentication? 2. What is authorization? 3. How are authentication and authorization different? 4. Why can a frontend route guard not provide complete security? 5. What is a session? Level 2 — Understanding 1. Describe a typical login flow from browser to backend. 2. Why must backend authorization be authoritative? 3. What is the purpose of a session or access token? 4. Why should protected UI routes still be backed by protected APIs? 5. What is the difference between identity and permission? Level 3 — Practical 1. Design a login/logout flow for JobHub. 2. Model authenticated user state. 3. Protect candidate, recruiter, and admin routes appropriately. 4. Design an authentication service boundary. 5. Define how session expiry should affect the UI. JobHub Scenarios 1. A user manually navigates to an admin URL. What should the frontend do, and what must the backend do? 2. A candidate changes the URL from candidate to recruiter. What security assumptions are unsafe? 3. A session expires while the user is editing a job. What recovery flow would you design? 4. A user is authenticated but lacks permission to publish jobs. How should the application represent that? Level 5 — Interviewer Follow Ups Can route guards secure an API? Where should role and permission checks happen? What is the difference between authentication state and authorization state? How would you test authentication architecture? Coding Question Design typed authentication state for JobHub, including anonymous, authenticated, and session expired states. Debugging Scenario An admin page is hidden by the UI but its API endpoint can still be called directly. Explain the missing security boundary. Common Interview Traps Treating route guards as security. Confusing login with authorization. Trusting client side role values. Storing sensitive secrets in frontend code. Project Connection — JobHub Authentication and authorization become the next major architectural layer after HTTP integration. Quick Revision Authentication establishes identity; authorization determines permissions; backend enforcement is the real security boundary. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can explain the complete identity to permission flow without relying on frontend checks as security.

title: Authentication Architecture
text: Day 121 — Authentication Architecture Interview Goal Understand how authentication fits into a modern Angular application without treating the frontend as the security boundary. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. What are the main parts of an authentication system? 2. What is the role of the frontend during login? 3. What is the role of the backend during authentication? 4. What is session state? 5. Why should authentication architecture be designed before building login UI? Level 2 — Understanding 1. Describe the flow from login form submission to an authenticated application. 2. Where should identity information come from? 3. Why should the frontend not decide whether credentials are valid? 4. What should happen when authentication fails? 5. How should an application represent an anonymous user? Level 3 — Practical 1. Design an AuthService boundary. 2. Define typed authenticated user state. 3. Define login and logout responsibilities. 4. Design application bootstrap behavior for an existing session. 5. Separate authentication state from authorization checks. JobHub Scenarios 1. JobHub supports Candidate, Recruiter, and Admin users. How would you model identity? 2. The browser reloads after login. How should the application restore session state? 3. Login succeeds but loading the current user fails. What state should the application enter? 4. A user opens a protected URL before authentication state finishes loading. How should navigation behave? Interviewer Follow Ups Authentication service versus auth store? Where should current user data come from? Why is backend identity authoritative? How would you test authentication bootstrap? Coding Question Design typed authentication states for anonymous, authenticating, authenticated, and authentication error conditions. Debugging Scenario The application briefly renders the protected dashboard before redirecting an anonymous user. Identify the missing authentication bootstrap state. Common Interview Traps Treating a local boolean as proof of authentication. Mixing authentication and authorization. Reading user roles from untrusted client state as the final authority. Ignoring application startup state. Project Connection — JobHub This architecture becomes the foundation for login, guards, permissions, interceptors, and authenticated feature shells. Quick Revision Authentication architecture coordinates identity, session state, bootstrap, login, logout, and failure handling. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can explain the authentication lifecycle before discussing individual Angular APIs.

title: Login, Logout and Session State
text: Day 122 — Login, Logout and Session State Interview Goal Implement predictable login/logout behavior and represent session state explicitly. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. What happens during login? 2. What happens during logout? 3. What is current user state? 4. Why should logout clear application state? 5. What is session expiry? Level 2 — Understanding 1. Why should login state not be represented only by the presence of a username in the UI? 2. What should happen to protected data after logout? 3. How should the application handle a failed login? 4. Why can logout require a backend request in some architectures? 5. How should a session expired state differ from an ordinary login failure? Level 3 — Practical 1. Build typed login and logout methods. 2. Model authenticated user state with Signals. 3. Expose computed authentication status. 4. Clear sensitive feature state on logout. 5. Design a session expiry transition. JobHub Scenarios 1. A recruiter logs out while the job editor is open. What state should be cleared? 2. Login succeeds but the dashboard API returns 401. What could have happened? 3. A session expires while browsing jobs. Should public job search remain available? 4. A logout request fails because the network is unavailable. What should the UI do? Interviewer Follow Ups Why use a computed authentication status? What state belongs in AuthService versus feature stores? How would you test logout cleanup? How should multiple browser tabs affect session state? Coding Question Create an AuthService with typed session state and login/logout methods using modern Angular Signals. Debugging Scenario The UI says "Logged out" but previously loaded recruiter data remains visible after logout. Identify the state cleanup problem. Common Interview Traps Clearing only the current user signal. Leaving protected feature state in memory. Assuming logout is always purely client side. Treating session expiry as the same as invalid credentials. Project Connection — JobHub Session state controls access to candidate, recruiter, and admin experiences. Quick Revision Login establishes session state; logout and expiry must also clean up protected application state. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can describe every meaningful transition in the session lifecycle.

title: Route Guards for Authentication
text: Day 123 — Route Guards for Authentication Interview Goal Use Angular route guards to control navigation while understanding their security limitations. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. What is a route guard? 2. Why would JobHub need an authentication guard? 3. What should a guard return? 4. What is a redirect from a guard? 5. Can a route guard secure a backend API? Level 2 — Understanding 1. Compare authentication guards with authorization guards. 2. Why should guards depend on application authentication state? 3. What should happen when authentication state is still loading? 4. Why should a guard return a navigation result rather than relying on unnecessary imperative navigation? 5. Why should backend APIs still enforce authentication? Level 3 — Practical 1. Create a functional authentication guard. 2. Protect the recruiter area. 3. Preserve the requested URL for post login navigation. 4. Handle an unknown authentication state. 5. Test allowed and blocked navigation. JobHub Scenarios 1. An anonymous user opens /recruiter/jobs/new. What should happen? 2. A logged in candidate opens an admin route. Which concern does an auth guard solve, and which does it not? 3. Authentication state loads asynchronously during navigation. How should the guard coordinate with it? 4. A user logs in after being redirected from a deep link. How should the original URL be restored? Interviewer Follow Ups Functional guard versus class based guard? Can guards make HTTP calls? What happens if multiple guards protect one route? How would you test a guard with RouterTestingHarness? Coding Question Implement a functional auth guard that redirects anonymous users to /login while preserving the intended destination. Debugging Scenario The guard always redirects because it reads the authentication signal before session bootstrap completes. Identify the state model problem. Common Interview Traps Treating guards as API security. Imperatively navigating inside guards unnecessarily. Ignoring asynchronous bootstrap. Forgetting deep link restoration. Project Connection — JobHub Authentication guards protect candidate, recruiter, and admin navigation boundaries. Quick Revision Guards improve navigation control and UX; backend authorization remains the actual security boundary. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can implement a guard and explain exactly what it cannot secure.

title: Role and Permission-Based Access
text: Day 124 — Role and Permission Based Access Interview Goal Understand authorization modeling beyond simple authenticated/not authenticated checks. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. What is a role? 2. What is a permission? 3. Why are roles and permissions different? 4. What is role based access control? 5. Why should frontend authorization be treated as a UX concern as well as a security concern? Level 2 — Understanding 1. Compare role checks with permission checks. 2. Why can a user have multiple roles or permissions? 3. Why should permission names be centralized? 4. How should the UI behave when a user lacks permission? 5. Why must the backend independently enforce permissions? Level 3 — Practical 1. Define typed JobHub roles. 2. Define typed permissions such as jobs.create, jobs.publish, and users.manage. 3. Build a reusable permission checking abstraction. 4. Protect routes based on permissions. 5. Hide or disable actions based on permission without treating that as security. JobHub Scenarios 1. Two recruiters can create jobs, but only senior recruiters can publish them. How would you model that? 2. An admin can manage users but not necessarily billing. Why might permissions be more useful than one large Admin role? 3. A user loses a permission while the application is open. How should the UI respond? 4. A button is hidden, but the API still accepts the action. What backend control is missing? Interviewer Follow Ups RBAC versus permission based authorization? Where should permission definitions live? Can the frontend safely calculate permissions? How would you test permission driven UI? Coding Question Create a typed permission model and a reusable hasPermission abstraction for JobHub. Debugging Scenario A candidate can see the recruiter route after changing a local role value. Explain why client side role data is not an authorization boundary. Common Interview Traps Treating hidden UI as security. Hard coding role checks throughout templates. Using strings everywhere without a centralized permission model. Assuming one role always maps to one fixed permission set. Project Connection — JobHub Permission modeling prepares JobHub for recruiter workflows and admin access management. Quick Revision Roles group responsibilities; permissions describe allowed actions; backend enforcement remains authoritative. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can design authorization around capabilities instead of scattered role checks.

title: Authentication Interceptors and Token Flow
text: Day 125 — Authentication Interceptors and Token Flow Interview Goal Understand how authenticated HTTP requests interact with Angular interceptors and session lifecycle. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. Why might an interceptor attach authentication information? 2. What is a token based authentication flow? 3. What happens when an authenticated API returns 401? 4. Why should token handling be centralized? 5. What is token refresh at a high level? Level 2 — Understanding 1. Describe a request flow from an authenticated component to a protected API. 2. What should an interceptor do when no session exists? 3. Why can blindly retrying a 401 create loops? 4. Why should refresh logic be designed separately from ordinary API calls? 5. What should happen if refresh fails? Level 3 — Practical 1. Build a conditional authentication interceptor. 2. Exclude public requests where required. 3. Detect authentication failures. 4. Coordinate session expiry handling. 5. Avoid duplicate refresh attempts. JobHub Scenarios 1. Ten requests fail with 401 at the same time. How could a naive refresh implementation create problems? 2. A public job search API returns 401 unexpectedly. What should the interceptor do? 3. Refresh fails. How should the application transition the user back to authentication? 4. A request is retried after refresh but still returns 401. What should stop the retry loop? Interviewer Follow Ups What is the difference between access and refresh tokens? Where should refresh tokens be stored? Should every 401 trigger refresh? How would you test concurrent 401 handling? Coding Question Design an interceptor flow that handles authenticated requests and transitions to session expiry without infinite retries. Debugging Scenario An application enters an infinite loop after a 401 response. Identify possible interceptor retry and refresh mistakes. Common Interview Traps Infinite 401 retry loops. Refreshing public requests. Duplicating auth logic in services. Treating token storage as a purely frontend security decision. Project Connection — JobHub The auth interceptor connects session state to the HTTP layer used by protected job operations. Quick Revision Authentication interceptors coordinate transport level identity handling; they do not replace backend authorization. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can reason about 401, refresh, retry, and session expiry transitions.

title: Authentication Storage and Security
text: Day 126 — Authentication Storage and Security Interview Goal Understand the security trade offs involved in browser side authentication state and credential storage. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. Where can browser applications store client side state? 2. What is localStorage? 3. What is sessionStorage? 4. What are cookies? 5. Why is sensitive credential storage a security concern? Level 2 — Understanding 1. Compare common browser storage mechanisms from a security perspective. 2. Why does XSS affect browser stored tokens? 3. What security properties can HttpOnly cookies provide? 4. Why does cookie based authentication introduce CSRF considerations? 5. Why should the frontend never treat storage contents as trusted identity? Level 3 — Practical 1. Document a session storage strategy for JobHub. 2. Minimize sensitive data stored in browser accessible storage. 3. Design logout cleanup. 4. Define secure cookie expectations for a backend team. 5. Document assumptions instead of claiming one storage method is universally safest. JobHub Scenarios 1. A team wants to store a long lived access token in localStorage. What risks should be reviewed? 2. The backend uses HttpOnly cookies. What frontend behavior changes? 3. A user shares a computer. What session behavior should the application consider? 4. Sensitive profile information remains in browser cache after logout. How should it be cleared or avoided? Interviewer Follow Ups HttpOnly versus localStorage? Secure and SameSite cookie attributes? Why does CSRF matter with cookies? Can frontend storage ever be treated as a secret store? Coding Question Design a documented authentication storage strategy for JobHub, including logout and threat assumptions. Debugging Scenario A token is readable from JavaScript even though the team expected it to be protected from script access. Identify the storage/configuration issue. Common Interview Traps Calling localStorage a secure token vault. Ignoring XSS. Ignoring CSRF for cookie sessions. Storing more sensitive information than the UI needs. Project Connection — JobHub Storage decisions affect the security architecture of every authenticated feature. Quick Revision Browser storage is a security boundary with trade offs; never treat client side data as inherently trusted. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can compare storage choices using explicit threat assumptions rather than slogans.

title: Authentication Errors and Session Expiry
text: Day 127 — Authentication Errors and Session Expiry Interview Goal Design graceful behavior when authentication fails, expires, or becomes invalid. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. What is session expiry? 2. What is the difference between invalid credentials and an expired session? 3. What does HTTP 401 commonly indicate? 4. What is the difference between 401 and 403 at a high level? 5. Why should users receive actionable authentication feedback? Level 2 — Understanding 1. What should happen when the session expires during an API request? 2. How should the application avoid redirecting repeatedly? 3. When should the user see a login screen versus an access denied screen? 4. Why should unsaved work be considered during session expiry? 5. How can the application preserve safe navigation context? Level 3 — Practical 1. Model session expired state. 2. Handle a 401 through the HTTP layer. 3. Redirect to login once. 4. Preserve a safe return URL. 5. Clear protected state after session invalidation. JobHub Scenarios 1. A recruiter spends 20 minutes editing a job and the session expires. What should the UX consider? 2. A candidate receives 403 when trying to publish a job. What does that communicate differently from 401? 3. Multiple API calls fail after session expiry. How should the app avoid multiple login redirects? 4. A session expires on an admin screen. What data must be cleared? Interviewer Follow Ups 401 versus 403? How would you preserve unsaved form data safely? Where should redirect coordination live? How would you test concurrent expiry events? Coding Question Design a session expiry handler that clears protected state and redirects to login without creating a redirect loop. Debugging Scenario Five failed API requests create five login navigations. Identify the missing coordination mechanism. Common Interview Traps Treating 401 and 403 as identical. Losing all unsaved work without considering recovery. Redirecting from every interceptor independently. Leaving protected data in memory after logout. Project Connection — JobHub Session expiry handling connects authentication, forms, HTTP errors, routing, and state management. Quick Revision Authentication failure handling is a coordinated application state transition, not merely an HTTP error message. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can design a single, recoverable session expiry flow.

title: Authenticated App Shell and UX
text: Day 128 — Authenticated App Shell and UX Interview Goal Design an application shell that changes safely according to authentication and authorization state. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. What is an authenticated app shell? 2. What UI usually belongs in an authenticated shell? 3. Why should public and protected layouts be separated? 4. What should a user see while authentication state is loading? 5. Why should navigation reflect permissions? Level 2 — Understanding 1. Compare public landing pages, login pages, and authenticated application shells. 2. How should navigation items be generated from capabilities? 3. Why should shell rendering wait for required session state? 4. How should the shell react to logout? 5. What should happen to feature routes after session expiry? Level 3 — Practical 1. Create public and authenticated route layouts. 2. Build a user/profile menu from authenticated state. 3. Show navigation based on permissions. 4. Add a session expiry transition. 5. Keep shell UI separate from feature business logic. JobHub Scenarios 1. Candidates see Candidate navigation while recruiters see Recruiter navigation. How should the shell determine visibility? 2. Admin navigation loads before permissions are known. What should the UI show? 3. User logs out from the profile menu. Which shell elements should disappear immediately? 4. A user has access to a route but not to one action on that page. How should navigation and action level permissions differ? Interviewer Follow Ups Shell versus feature layout? How should navigation state be tested? Should hidden menu items be considered authorization? How would you prevent shell logic from becoming a monolith? Coding Question Design an authenticated JobHub shell with permission aware navigation and explicit loading, authenticated, and anonymous states. Debugging Scenario The shell displays recruiter navigation for a candidate until a second render. Identify the race between session bootstrap and navigation computation. Common Interview Traps Rendering protected navigation before identity is known. Putting all feature logic in the shell. Treating menu visibility as security. Duplicating permission logic in every menu item. Project Connection — JobHub The authenticated shell becomes the stable container for candidate, recruiter, and admin features. Quick Revision The app shell should reflect session and capability state while remaining independent of feature specific business logic. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can design shell behavior for anonymous, loading, authenticated, expired, and unauthorized states.

title: Mini Project: Authenticated Job Portal
text: Day 129 — Mini Project: Authenticated Job Portal Interview Goal Combine authentication, authorization, routing, HTTP, and shell UX into one realistic feature. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. What features should an authenticated job portal contain? 2. Which routes are public? 3. Which routes require authentication? 4. Which actions require specific permissions? 5. What should happen when the session expires? Level 2 — Understanding 1. Describe the complete login to dashboard flow. 2. Where should authentication state live? 3. Where should permission checks live? 4. Where should authentication headers be added? 5. Which parts must be enforced by the backend? Level 3 — Practical 1. Build login and logout. 2. Protect authenticated routes. 3. Add role/permission aware navigation. 4. Add an authenticated app shell. 5. Add session expiry handling. 6. Connect protected APIs through an auth aware HTTP layer. JobHub Scenarios 1. Candidate and recruiter share job search screens but have different actions. How should authorization work? 2. A recruiter can create jobs but cannot publish them. How should UI and backend coordinate? 3. The session expires while the user is submitting an application. How should the workflow recover? 4. A user manually requests an admin API. What must prevent unauthorized access? Interviewer Follow Ups What would you test end to end? Which concerns belong in guards, interceptors, services, and backend APIs? How would you handle multiple simultaneous 401 responses? How would you explain this architecture in an interview? Coding Question Implement the core authenticated Job Portal flow with typed session state, route guards, permission aware navigation, and protected API access. Debugging Scenario A candidate can navigate to the recruiter area after changing a local role value, but recruiter API calls fail. Explain why frontend role checks are not sufficient. Common Interview Traps Putting all auth logic in route guards. Treating hidden UI as security. Duplicating token handling. Forgetting session expiry and logout cleanup. Project Connection — JobHub This mini project closes the Authentication module and becomes the security foundation for the complete Angular capstone. Quick Revision A secure Angular application coordinates identity, navigation, permissions, HTTP, state, and backend enforcement. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can draw the authentication flow and explain every boundary.

title: Project Planning and Requirements
text: Day 130 — Project Planning and Requirements Interview Goal Begin the complete JobHub Angular project by translating requirements into features, boundaries, and deliverables. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. Why should a project be planned before implementation? 2. What is a functional requirement? 3. What is a non functional requirement? 4. Why are user roles important in application planning? 5. What is a feature boundary? Level 2 — Understanding 1. Convert a job platform idea into candidate, recruiter, and admin capabilities. 2. Separate user stories from technical implementation details. 3. Identify dependencies between features. 4. Identify performance, accessibility, security, and responsive requirements. 5. Why should API assumptions be documented early? Level 3 — Practical 1. Write JobHub functional requirements. 2. Define primary user journeys. 3. Create an initial feature map. 4. Identify required API capabilities. 5. Define acceptance criteria for major features. JobHub Scenarios 1. Candidate can search, save, and apply; recruiter can create and manage jobs; admin manages users and permissions. How would you partition these capabilities? 2. Which requirements are essential for the first project increment? 3. Which features can be implemented independently? 4. Which requirements create cross feature dependencies? Interviewer Follow Ups How do requirements affect Angular architecture? How do you prevent scope from expanding uncontrollably? What makes a good acceptance criterion? How would you communicate technical constraints to stakeholders? Coding Question Create a feature map for JobHub showing candidate, recruiter, admin, shared, and platform capabilities. Debugging Scenario Developers start building components before agreeing on roles and workflows, causing repeated rewrites. What planning step was missing? Common Interview Traps Starting from UI screens instead of user journeys. Mixing implementation details with requirements. Ignoring non functional requirements. Treating backend contracts as an afterthought. Project Connection — JobHub Day 130 turns the previous Angular concepts into a structured capstone plan. Quick Revision Good project planning defines users, workflows, requirements, boundaries, dependencies, and acceptance criteria before implementation. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can turn an application idea into implementable, testable requirements.

title: Application Architecture and Folder Structure
text: Day 131 — Application Architecture and Folder Structure Interview Goal Explain and apply the architecture concepts from this capstone day in a production Angular application. Level 1 — Basic Questions 1. What is the main problem this topic solves in a growing Angular application? 2. Which Angular concepts from earlier modules does this topic depend on? 3. What responsibilities should remain separate? 4. Why does strict typing improve this design? Level 2 — Understanding 1. Explain the trade offs involved in the design. 2. Compare a simple implementation with an enterprise scale implementation. 3. What belongs to the UI, feature, service, state, and API layers? 4. How would you keep the design testable? Level 3 — Practical 1. Design the solution for JobHub using standalone components and modern Angular APIs. 2. Identify the state, data flow, and failure states involved. 3. Explain how you would structure the TypeScript contracts. 4. Describe how you would prevent unnecessary coupling. JobHub Scenarios Feature boundaries, core/shared/domain/features, typed public APIs, dependency direction, and JobHub folder architecture. Practical questions: design Candidate/Recruiter/Admin structure; decide where API models, UI models, auth infrastructure, and shared business logic belong; explain how to prevent feature to feature internal imports. Coding: create a strict TypeScript feature structure and public API. Debugging: resolve circular dependencies caused by cross feature imports. Interviewer Follow Ups What would you change if JobHub grew from a small application to a multi team enterprise product? How would you test this design? What failure modes would you expect in production? Which responsibility should remain on the backend? Coding Question Implement a small, strictly typed version of the core design from this day. Prefer standalone Angular APIs, input/output signals where appropriate, inject(), and modern control flow. Debugging Scenario A feature works initially but becomes difficult to maintain because UI logic, API calls, state, and authorization have become tightly coupled. Explain how you would isolate responsibilities and diagnose the dependency problem. Common Interview Traps Over engineering before there is a real problem. Using any instead of strict domain types. Making every value global state. Treating frontend behavior as the backend security boundary. Mixing reusable UI with business specific logic. Project Connection — JobHub This day strengthens the production architecture of the JobHub capstone and connects earlier Angular fundamentals with enterprise implementation decisions. Quick Revision Review the topic, its boundaries, the JobHub scenario, the coding exercise, and the failure/debugging case. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can explain not only how to implement the feature, but also why each responsibility belongs where you placed it.

title: Job Search and Filtering

Prefer explicit tool contracts, narrow permissions, typed inputs/outputs, and clear separation between UI, application services, backend authorization, and AI infrastructure. Interview Questions What is the difference between AI assisted development and an AI powered application? What is MCP, and what problem does it solve? How is Angular CLI MCP different from WebMCP? Why should experimental APIs be isolated behind clear boundaries? Why must an AI tool not automatically become a security boundary? How would you prevent an AI agent from performing an unauthorized JobHub action? Coding Question Implement a small typed Angular example related to today's topic. Use standalone APIs, , signals where appropriate, and strict TypeScript. Do not use . Explain how you would inspect the generated code, verify the contract, reproduce the issue, fix it, and add regression coverage. Common Traps Treating AI output as trusted production code. Sending secrets or private data directly to a model from the browser. Giving an AI tool broader permissions than required. Confusing Angular CLI MCP with WebMCP. Treating experimental WebMCP APIs as stable Angular fundamentals. Skipping schema/input validation because an agent generated the request. Allowing the AI layer to bypass normal backend authorization. Building AI functionality where deterministic Angular logic is sufficient. Project Connection — JobHub Use JobHub as the running example. AI may help developers build JobHub, while AI powered JobHub features can assist candidates or recruiters. Keep these two concerns separate. text: Day 335 — Mini Project — AI Powered Job Assistant Learning Goal Combine Angular AI development, MCP concepts, WebMCP experimentation, typed services, signals, forms, security, and tool calling into an AI powered JobHub assistant. Coding: design and present the complete architecture, tool contracts, UX, testing, and security model. Core Concepts 1. What problem does this AI capability solve? 2. How does it relate to Angular's application and developer tooling? 3. What belongs in Angular, what belongs in the backend, and what belongs in the AI/tooling layer? 4. Which APIs are stable, experimental, or provider specific? Practical Angular Questions 1. How would you implement this in a standalone Angular application? 2. How would you keep the design strongly typed? 3. How would you test the behavior without depending on a live model or agent? 4. How would you handle failures, latency, permissions, and unavailable AI services? JobHub Scenario Design a realistic JobHub use case for today's topic. Prefer explicit tool contracts, narrow permissions, typed inputs/outputs, and clear separation between UI, application services, backend authorization, and AI infrastructure. Interview Questions What is the difference between AI assisted development and an AI powered application? What is MCP, and what problem does it solve? How is Angular CLI MCP different from WebMCP? Why should experimental APIs be isolated behind clear boundaries? Why must an AI tool not automatically become a security boundary? How would you prevent an AI agent from performing an unauthorized JobHub action? Coding Question Implement a small typed Angular example related to today's topic. Use standalone APIs, , signals where appropriate, and strict TypeScript. Do not use . Debugging Scenario An AI generated Angular feature compiles but violates project architecture, exposes sensitive data, registers duplicate tools, uses an experimental API incorrectly, or performs an unauthorized action. Explain how you would inspect the generated code, verify the contract, reproduce the issue, fix it, and add regression coverage. Common Traps Treating AI output as trusted production code. Sending secrets or private data directly to a model from the browser. Giving an AI tool broader permissions than required. Confusing Angular CLI MCP with WebMCP. Treating experimental WebMCP APIs as stable Angular fundamentals. Skipping schema/input validation because an agent generated the request. Allowing the AI layer to bypass normal backend authorization. Building AI functionality where deterministic Angular logic is sufficient. Project Connection — JobHub Use JobHub as the running example. AI may help developers build JobHub, while AI powered JobHub features can assist candidates or recruiters. Keep these two concerns separate. Quick Revision Review the AI problem, Angular boundary, MCP/tool contract, data flow, security model, testing strategy, and experimental/stable status. Interview Readiness You are ready when you can explain the feature without hype, distinguish framework capabilities from third party AI providers, write a typed implementation, and identify security and reliability risks.
